title: How animals breathe and find their food

summary.text: A rohu fish spends a whole life under water, yet breathes all day. Almost every animal needs oxygen, a gas found in air and dissolved in water, because their cells use it to get energy from food. Animals take oxygen in with lungs, gills, damp skin or tiny air pipes, and they breathe out carbon dioxide made from their food. To find that food, they use their senses, including some we do not have, like a bat's echolocation. Scientists still argue about how lungs first appeared, and why earthworms crawl out after rain.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a child breathing out a little cloud onto a cold steel tumbler, a fish with red gills and a frog with shiny wet skin. On the right, a dog sniffing, a bat sending out sound waves and an ant on a sugar trail.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a steel tumbler close to your mouth and breathe out on it slowly, three times. What appears on the steel? Your breath carries something out of your body. A fish breathes too, but under water. How does a fish do that?
intro.text: In summer, when village ponds in Bengal and Assam dry up, people sometimes dig in the damp mud and find fish still alive. One of them, the climbing perch, can live out of water for hours if they stay damp. They can even wriggle across wet grass to the next pond. They can do this because they breathe air as well as water. How does a fish breathe air? And how does any animal, in water, mud or sky, get the oxygen and the food they need?
intro.art: A cracked dry pond bed at dawn, a village child kneeling and holding up a small greenish fish from a hole in the mud, a fresh pond shining in the distance.

outcomes: I can say why animals need oxygen: almost every cell in their bodies uses oxygen to get energy from food.
I can explain how lungs, gills and skin each take in oxygen, and why all of them are thin, damp and close to blood.
I can count and compare my breaths before and after exercise, as a fair test, and say what the numbers show.
I can show that breathed-out air is different from room air, using limewater made from chuna.
I can name the senses animals use to find food, including senses people do not have, like echo-hearing and heat-sensing.
I can describe different ways animals get food: grazing, hunting, waiting, filtering, trapping and scavenging.
I can say what scientists agree about breathing, and what they still argue about.
I can explain that the oxygen I breathe was made by plants and algae, and that part of the food I eat leaves my body in my breath.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour and no smell. It is in air, and a little of it is dissolved in water. Animals need it to stay alive.
terms.example: Each time you breathe in, oxygen goes into your body.
terms.art: Air drawn as tiny dots, with a few dots coloured blue and labelled oxygen, flowing into a child's nose.

terms.meaning: A gas our bodies make and breathe out. Plants take it in and use it to make food.
terms.example: The fizz in a soda drink is carbon dioxide. You breathe out a little carbon dioxide all the time.
terms.art: A child breathing out grey dots towards a tulsi plant, which is drinking them in.

terms.meaning: Moving air or water in and out of the body, so that oxygen can get in and carbon dioxide can get out.
terms.example: Your chest rises when you breathe in, and falls when you breathe out.
terms.art: A child with a hand on the chest, the chest rising with an arrow up.

terms.meaning: What happens inside almost every cell: the cell uses oxygen to release the energy stored in food. It makes carbon dioxide and water as it does this. Breathing brings in the oxygen that respiration needs.
terms.example: When you run, your leg cells do more respiration, so you breathe faster.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle on a leg muscle showing a cell taking in oxygen and food and giving out a spark of energy.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that bodies are built from. Your body has many millions of millions of cells.
terms.example: Your skin, blood and muscles are all made of cells.
terms.art: A child's arm with a magnifying circle showing cells like small bricks.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy bags inside the chest. Air goes in and out of them. Oxygen passes from the lungs into the blood.
terms.example: People, dogs, crows, snakes and dolphins all have lungs.
terms.art: A simple drawing of two pink lungs in a child's chest, with the windpipe branching like a tree.

terms.meaning: Millions of tiny bubbles at the ends of the branches inside the lungs. Their walls are thinner than tissue paper. Oxygen passes through them into the blood.
terms.example: Your two lungs hold about 480 million air sacs, like a huge bunch of tiny grapes.
terms.art: A branch of the lung ending in a bunch of grape-like bubbles, each wrapped in red blood vessels.

terms.meaning: Feathery red parts on each side of a fish's head. Water flows over them, and they take oxygen out of the water.
terms.example: At a fish market, sellers lift the flap on a fish's head to show the bright red gills.
terms.art: A rohu fish with their gill flap lifted, showing rows of red feathery gills, and arrows of water flowing in at the mouth and out under the flap.

terms.meaning: The hard flap that covers a fish's gills. It opens and closes as water flows out.
terms.example: Watch a goldfish closely. The flaps behind their eyes open and shut all the time.
terms.art: A goldfish side-on with their gill cover slightly open.

terms.meaning: Taking in oxygen straight through the skin. It only works if the skin is thin and kept damp.
terms.example: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. They breathe only through their damp skin.
terms.art: An earthworm on damp soil with tiny blue dots passing into their skin.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes along the sides of an insect's body. Air goes in through them, into thin pipes that reach every part of the insect.
terms.example: A grasshopper has a row of spiracles along each side.
terms.art: A grasshopper close up, with a row of small dots along their side, and thin tubes branching inside.

terms.meaning: The nostril on top of the head of a dolphin or a whale. The animal breathes air through it when they come up to the surface.
terms.example: The Ganges river dolphin comes up to breathe through their blowhole every minute or two.
terms.art: A Ganges river dolphin breaking the brown river surface, a small puff of spray rising from their blowhole.

terms.meaning: The ways a body learns about the world: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. Some animals have extra senses that people do not have.
terms.example: A dog finds a hidden biscuit by smell.
terms.art: A dog with their nose to the ground, following a dotted smell trail to a biscuit under a cushion.

terms.meaning: Finding things by sending out sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back.
terms.example: Bats and dolphins find insects and fish in the dark this way.
terms.art: A bat at dusk sending out curved sound lines that bounce off a moth and come back to their ears.

terms.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A kingfisher is a predator. They dive to catch small fish.
terms.art: A kingfisher diving into a pond towards a small fish.

terms.meaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
terms.example: A small fish is the kingfisher's prey.
terms.art: A small silver fish darting away from a kingfisher's shadow.

terms.meaning: An animal that sieves tiny bits of food out of water.
terms.example: Flamingos sieve tiny shrimps and algae out of lake water with their beaks.
terms.art: A pink flamingo with their head upside down in shallow water, their beak working like a sieve.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats the bodies of animals that have already died.
terms.example: Vultures and crows are scavengers. They clean up dead animals.
terms.art: Two vultures on a dry field near a cow skeleton, a crow waiting nearby.

terms.meaning: Simple plant-like living things that live in water. Most of them are tiny. Like plants, they make food from sunlight and give out oxygen.
terms.example: The green colour in an old bucket of water is algae.
terms.art: A drop of pond water under a magnifier showing tiny green specks and threads.

terms.meaning: An extra breathing part above the gills of some fish, folded many times like a maze. It takes oxygen from air that the fish gulps at the surface.
terms.example: The climbing perch, called koi in Bengali, has a labyrinth organ. So does the betta fish sold in aquarium shops.
terms.art: A climbing perch with a cut-away above their gills showing a folded, maze-like breathing part, and a bubble of air at their mouth.

terms.meaning: Clear water with lime (calcium hydroxide) dissolved in it. It turns milky when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
terms.example: Edible chuna from a paan shop, stirred into water and left to settle, gives clear limewater.
terms.art: Two glasses of water, one clear and one milky white, with a child blowing bubbles through a straw into the milky one.

explanations.definition: Almost every cell in an animal's body uses oxygen to release the energy stored in food. This is called respiration. Breathing is how the body gets that oxygen in, and gets the carbon dioxide out.
explanations.description: Food is stored energy, a bit like wood waiting to be burned. To get the energy out, a cell needs oxygen, just as a fire needs air. The cell joins the food and oxygen slowly, in many small steps, with no flame. Out comes energy to move, grow, think and keep warm. Out also come carbon dioxide and water. The carbon in that carbon dioxide was part of the food. So breathing has two jobs. It brings oxygen in, and it takes carbon dioxide out. A cell that gets no oxygen soon stops working. That is why we cannot hold our breath for very long.
examples: When you run, your leg muscles use more oxygen, so you breathe faster.
A candle under an upturned glass goes out when the oxygen runs low. Cells use oxygen too, but slowly, without flames.
A sleeping dog breathes slowly. A dog that has just chased a ball pants.
explanations.art: A cell drawn as a little factory with doors: food and oxygen go in, energy sparks, carbon dioxide and water come out.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea behind all breathing: why animals need oxygen at all.

explanations.concept: What every breathing part has in common
explanations.definition: Lungs, gills and breathing skin all work in the same way. They are thin, they are damp, they have a very large surface for their size, and blood flows just underneath.
explanations.description: Oxygen can only get into the body by passing through a thin, wet wall. On the other side of that wall is blood, which carries the oxygen away to the cells. So the best breathing parts have very thin walls. They stay damp, because oxygen has to dissolve in a film of water before it can pass through. They are folded or branched many times, so they have a lot of surface. More surface lets more oxygen in at once. And blood is always flowing right next to them. Lungs, gills and frog skin look very different. Up close, they all work in the same way.
examples: A grown-up's lungs are folded into about 480 million tiny air sacs. Spread flat, they would cover roughly a badminton court.
A fish's gills are split into hundreds of thin, feathery threads.
A frog's skin is thin and slimy, with many tiny blood vessels underneath.
explanations.art: Three zoomed-in circles side by side: a lung air sac, a gill thread and frog skin, each a thin wall with oxygen dots passing into red blood underneath.
explanations.context: This card shows how lungs, gills and breathing skin are really the same idea underneath.

explanations.definition: Lungs are two spongy bags in the chest. A sheet of muscle under them, the diaphragm, pulls down to draw air in, and relaxes to let air out.
explanations.description: Air goes in through your nose or mouth and down a pipe called the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two, one branch for each lung. Each branch splits again and again, like the branches of a banyan tree. At the very tips are tiny air sacs. Oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood. Carbon dioxide passes the other way, out of the blood into the air sacs. Then you breathe it out. Your lungs cannot move by themselves. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under them, pulls down and makes space. Air rushes in to fill it. Breathed-out air still has some oxygen in it, but less than room air, and much more carbon dioxide.
examples: People, cows, crows, snakes, tortoises and dolphins all breathe with lungs.
A dolphin's lungs fill through a blowhole on top of their head.
Room air is about 21 parts in 100 oxygen. Breathed-out air is about 16 parts in 100. Room air has only a tiny bit of carbon dioxide. Breathed-out air has about 100 times as much.
explanations.art: A child's body outline with the windpipe branching into two lungs like an upside-down tree, and a dome-shaped diaphragm below, with arrows showing it pull down.
explanations.context: This card explains how lungs work, from the nose to the tiny air sacs.

explanations.definition: Gills take oxygen out of water. A fish gulps water in through their mouth. The water flows over the gills and out under the gill covers.
explanations.description: Water holds far less oxygen than air, about thirty times less in the same space. So a fish must be very good at catching it. Their gills are rows of thin red threads, each covered in even thinner folds. Blood flows through them the opposite way to the water. Because of this, the blood keeps meeting water that has more oxygen than it has. So a fish can take most of the oxygen out of the water that passes over it. Out of water, the soft gill threads stick together, like a wet paintbrush pulled out of a jar. Then there is too little surface, and the fish cannot breathe. That is why most fish die in air, even though air has more oxygen than water.
examples: Rohu, catla and goldfish breathe with gills.
Tadpoles breathe with gills. Most grow lungs when they become frogs.
Crabs and prawns breathe with gills too, tucked under their hard shells.
explanations.art: A fish's head cut away to show water arrows flowing in at the mouth, over red gill threads, and out under the gill cover, with blood arrows going the other way.
explanations.context: This card explains how fish take oxygen out of water with their gills.

explanations.definition: Some animals take in oxygen straight through their skin. Their skin must be thin and kept damp, or the oxygen cannot pass through.
explanations.description: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. Oxygen from the air between soil crumbs passes straight through their moist skin into their blood. If an earthworm dries out in the sun, they can no longer breathe. Frogs have lungs, but they also breathe through their skin. A frog resting underwater in a pond in winter can get all the oxygen they need through their skin. Some salamanders, a group of animals related to frogs, have no lungs at all. In 2008 scientists found the first frog known to have no lungs. This frog lives in cold, fast streams in Borneo. Fast, cold water holds plenty of oxygen, so their skin is enough.
examples: An earthworm breathes only through their skin.
A frog breathes with lungs and with their skin.
Mudskippers, the fish that hop on the mud in Indian mangroves, take in oxygen through their skin and the inside of their mouths.
explanations.art: An earthworm in a cross-section of damp soil, a frog half in a pond, and a flat-headed frog in a rushing stream, each with small oxygen dots passing into the skin.
explanations.context: This card explains animals that breathe through their skin, like earthworms and frogs.

explanations.definition: Insects breathe through holes in their sides called spiracles, and air pipes that reach every part of the body. Some fish can breathe air as well as water.
explanations.description: An insect has no lungs. Air goes in through small holes along their sides. It travels down thin pipes that branch again and again until they reach every tiny part of the body. So in an insect, air goes straight to the cells. Some fish live in warm, muddy ponds where the water has little oxygen. The climbing perch, called koi in Bengali, has an extra breathing part above their gills, folded like a maze. It is called the labyrinth organ. The fish gulps air at the surface, and the labyrinth organ takes oxygen from it. So they can stay alive out of water for hours, if they stay damp. The magur and singhi catfish sold alive in Indian markets can also breathe air. That is why they stay alive in a bucket with very little water.
examples: A grasshopper breathes through spiracles along their sides.
A young mosquito, called a larva, lives in water. They breathe air through a tiny tube that they poke up through the surface.
The climbing perch can wriggle across wet grass from one pond to another.
explanations.art: A grasshopper with their air pipes drawn like branching silver threads, next to a climbing perch with a maze-like labyrinth organ above their gills, gulping air at a pond's surface.
explanations.context: This card shows more ways animals breathe: insects' air pipes and fish that gulp air.

explanations.definition: Animals that breathe air but hunt underwater must hold their breath. Animals that fly very high must get oxygen from thin air.
explanations.description: Dolphins, whales, turtles and otters breathe with lungs, so they must come up for air. The Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal, comes up every minute or two. Some deep-diving whales can stay under for more than an hour. One Cuvier's beaked whale was recorded staying under for 222 minutes, nearly four hours. They store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles, and slow their hearts while they dive. High in the sky, the air is thin, so each breath has less oxygen. Bar-headed geese fly right over the Himalayas to spend the winter in India. Their blood picks up oxygen more easily than ours. They also have big lungs, take very deep breaths and have strong hearts.
examples: A Ganges river dolphin surfaces every minute or two to breathe.
A sea turtle can sleep underwater for hours, because a resting body uses little oxygen.
Bar-headed geese cross the Himalayas twice a year.
explanations.art: A Ganges river dolphin surfacing in a brown river, and high above the snowy Himalayas a V of bar-headed geese.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that hold their breath for a long time, or breathe very thin air.

explanations.concept: How animals find food: their senses
explanations.definition: Animals find food with their senses. Different animals rely on different senses, depending on where and how they live.
explanations.description: A dog finds food mostly by smell. Their nose has many times more smell cells than yours. An eagle finds food mostly by sight, spotting a mouse from high in the sky. An owl can catch a mouse in the dark just by hearing the mouse rustle. A cat's whiskers feel tiny movements of air, which helps them in the dark. Some animals have senses we do not have at all. Bats and Ganges river dolphins send out clicks and listen to the echoes. Sharks feel the tiny electricity made by the muscles of hidden fish. Pit vipers, like the Malabar pit viper of the Western Ghats, have pits on their faces that sense the warmth of a mouse in the dark.
examples: Ants find food by smell, and leave a smell trail for other ants to follow.
A mosquito finds you by the carbon dioxide you breathe out, and by your warmth.
A honeybee sees colours on flowers that we cannot see.
explanations.art: A row of animals each with one glowing sense: a dog's nose, an eagle's eye, an owl's ears, a cat's whiskers, a bat's sound waves and a snake's heat pits.
explanations.context: This card explains how animals use their senses to find food.

explanations.definition: Animals get food in many different ways. Some graze, some hunt, some wait, some sieve, some build traps and some clean up the dead.
explanations.description: A cow grazes. She walks slowly and eats grass for hours. A cheetah hunts. They chase their prey at great speed. A crocodile waits. They lie still in the river until an animal comes close. A flamingo filters. They sieve tiny shrimps and algae out of lake water. A spider builds a trap. Their sticky web catches flying insects. A vulture scavenges. They eat animals that have already died, and so cleans up the land. Each way of eating goes with a body that fits it. A cow has flat teeth for grinding. A cheetah has long legs and a flexible back for running fast. A flamingo has a beak that works like a sieve.
examples: A sunbird sips nectar from flowers with their long, thin, curved beak.
A whale shark, the biggest fish, filters tiny food out of seawater.
An antlion digs a pit in dry sand and waits at the bottom for ants to fall in.
explanations.art: Six small scenes in a grid: a cow grazing, a cheetah running, a crocodile waiting, a flamingo filtering, a spider's web and a vulture.
explanations.context: This card explains the different ways animals get their food.

explanations.concept: Smell may be the oldest sense
explanations.description: Long before there were eyes or ears, the first living things were single cells living in water. Even today, a bacterium senses sugar in the water around them and decides to swim towards it. They also swim away from harmful chemicals. Sensing chemicals is a kind of smelling and tasting. So many scientists think that sensing chemicals is the oldest way of finding food. Smell and taste may be the oldest senses of all. There is a lot of evidence for this, but nobody was there to watch, so we call it an idea.
examples: Under a microscope, bacteria swim towards a drop of sugar.
A tiny single-celled creature in pond water turns towards food.
Ants and termites still use smell to find food and talk to each other.
explanations.art: A drop of water under a microscope with tiny bacteria all swimming towards a sugar crystal at one side.
explanations.context: This card shares an idea about the very first way living things found food.

explanations.description: Long ago, all animals with backbones lived in water and breathed with gills. Some fish lived in warm, muddy swamps with little oxygen. They began to gulp air into a pouch in their throats. Over a very long time, these pouches became lungs. Many fish today have a gas bag instead, called a swim bladder, which helps them float. Which came first, the lung or the swim bladder? Scientists have argued about this.
examples: Lungfish, which still live in Africa, South America and Australia, have lungs and gills.
A goldfish has a swim bladder. It helps them float without sinking or rising.
Bichirs, an old kind of African fish, have simple lungs.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, in his book On the Origin of Species (1859)
perspectives.explanation: Darwin thought the swim bladder of fish came first, and slowly changed into the lungs of land animals.

Studies of old kinds of fish, like bichirs and lungfish, and of fossils, suggest the opposite. Lungs came first, in early fish. Later, in many fish, the lung changed into a swim bladder for floating. Most scientists now lean this way, but the details are still being studied.

explanations.art: A muddy ancient swamp with a fish poking their mouth above the water to gulp air, and a cut-away of their throat showing a small air pouch.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle: did lungs come from fish swim bladders, or the other way round?

explanations.concept: Why do earthworms come out when it rains?
explanations.description: After heavy rain, you often see earthworms lying on paths and roads. Earthworms breathe through their skin, so many people think they come up to stop drowning. But earthworms can live under water for a long time if the water has oxygen in it. So scientists are not sure. There are several ideas, and maybe more than one is true.
examples: Earthworms on a wet road in the monsoon.
In experiments, earthworms have stayed alive under water for a long time when the water had oxygen in it.
Some fishermen in other countries drum on the ground to call worms up.

perspectives.explanation: Water soaking the soil may hold less oxygen than air did. The worms come up to breathe more easily.
When everything is wet, worms can crawl far over the surface without drying out. Rain is a good time to move to a new place.
The drumming of rain may feel like the digging of a mole, which eats worms. The worms crawl up to escape it. People who drum on the ground to call worms up support this idea.

explanations.art: A wet path in the monsoon with several earthworms on it, and three thought bubbles above them: a bubble, a road, and a mole.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle nobody has fully solved: why earthworms crawl out after rain.

agreed.text: Almost all animals need oxygen, and they give out carbon dioxide.
agreed.evidence: Animals kept in a sealed box with no fresh air soon struggle. Scientists can measure the oxygen going in and the carbon dioxide coming out of any animal, from a mouse to a beetle. The only known exception is a tiny animal that lives inside fish muscle, found in 2020, which does not use oxygen.

agreed.text: Lungs, gills and breathing skin all work the same way: oxygen passes through a thin, damp wall into blood.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, the walls of air sacs, gill threads and frog skin are all very thin, with tiny blood vessels right underneath.

agreed.text: Breathed-out air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than room air.
agreed.evidence: Limewater, which you can make from chuna, turns milky with carbon dioxide. It turns milky fast with breathed-out air, and very slowly with room air. Machines in hospitals measure the same thing.

agreed.text: Animals breathe faster when they are active, because their muscles use more oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Count anyone's breaths before and after running, and you get the same pattern. Doctors use this in fitness tests.

agreed.text: Animals find food with their senses, and different animals rely on different senses.
agreed.evidence: Experiments show that bats with their ears blocked crash into things, while dogs can follow a smell trail that is days old.

agreed.text: The oxygen in air was made by living things: plants on land and tiny algae in the sea.
agreed.evidence: Ancient rocks show that there was almost no oxygen in the air until tiny living things in the sea, called cyanobacteria, began to make it, more than two billion years ago.

agreed.text: Much of the food an animal eats leaves their body as carbon dioxide in their breath.
agreed.evidence: Cells break food down with oxygen, and the carbon in the food comes out as carbon dioxide. In 2014, Ruben Meerman and Andrew Brown worked out that most of the fat a person loses leaves through the lungs as carbon dioxide.

challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and some adults
challenging.for: Fish never come up for air, and we cannot see them breathing.
challenging.against: Fish breathe all the time. Watch a fish in a tank. Their mouth and gill covers open and shut, pumping water over the gills. The gills take oxygen out of the water.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that fish do not need to breathe.

challenging.claim: We breathe in oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.
challenging.who: A common way of saying it, even in some books
challenging.for: It is a simple way to remember breathing.
challenging.against: Breathed-out air still has plenty of oxygen, about 16 parts in 100, compared with 21 parts in room air. That is why rescue breathing, when a person breathes into someone who has stopped breathing, can work. Breathed-out air is mostly nitrogen, just like room air. It has a little less oxygen, about 100 times more carbon dioxide, and more water.
challenging.context: This card is about a common way of describing breathing, and why it is not quite right.

challenging.who: An old saying, as blind as a bat
challenging.for: Bats fly at night, and many have small eyes.
challenging.against: Bats can see. Many fruit bats see very well, and insect-eating bats also use echolocation. In the 1790s, the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani found that bats could still fly in the dark with their eyes covered. The Swiss surgeon Louis Jurine then found that bats lost their way when their ears were blocked. Around 1940, Donald Griffin and Robert Galambos showed that bats use sounds too high for us to hear.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that bats are blind, and how scientists found out the truth.

challenging.claim: Whales and dolphins are fish, because they live in water.
challenging.who: A common idea, and an old way of sorting animals
challenging.for: They live in water and have fish-like shapes.
challenging.against: Whales and dolphins breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole. They would drown if they could not reach the surface. Their babies drink milk. Living in water is not the same as breathing water.
challenging.context: This card is about whether dolphins and whales breathe like fish.

challenging.who: Lieutenant Daldorff, a Danish officer at Tranquebar in Tamil Nadu, who wrote in the 1790s that he saw one high in a palm tree
challenging.for: The fish can breathe air and wriggle across land, using the spines on their gill covers. Their scientific name, Anabas, means 'climbing up'.
challenging.against: Nobody has reliably seen one climb a tree since. Many scientists think birds like kites and crows caught the fish, carried them to trees and dropped them. Because the fish breathes air, they could still be alive up there, which made them look like a climber.
challenging.context: This card is about an old report that a fish climbed a palm tree, and what scientists think now.

challenging.claim: The tiny parts that use oxygen inside your cells were once free-living bacteria.
challenging.who: Lynn Margulis, an American biologist, in 1967. Her paper was turned down by many journals before it was published.
challenging.for: These tiny parts, called mitochondria, use oxygen just as some bacteria do. They even have their own little bit of DNA, like bacteria.
challenging.against: At first, most biologists thought the idea was strange and unlikely. But DNA tests later showed that mitochondria really did come from bacteria that moved into bigger cells long ago.
challenging.context: This card is about a once-mocked idea about where our cells' breathing parts came from.

big_questions.q: If a fish has gills that take oxygen from water, why does the fish die in air, which has much more oxygen?
big_questions.hint: Think of a wet paintbrush taken out of water. What happens to its soft hairs?

big_questions.q: Where was the oxygen in your last breath a week ago?
big_questions.hint: Who puts oxygen into the air? Think of trees, grass and the green algae in ponds and seas.

big_questions.q: If almost every cell in you uses oxygen, which part of you is really doing the breathing: your nose, your lungs or your cells?
big_questions.hint: Your nose and lungs are like doors. Where does the oxygen finally go?

big_questions.q: A dog smells a world we cannot smell. A bat hears echoes we cannot hear. Is the world we see the whole world?
big_questions.hint: Think of all the senses other animals have that we do not.

big_questions.q: Part of the lunch you ate today will leave in your breath as carbon dioxide. A plant may then take it in. Is that leaf then partly made from your lunch?
big_questions.hint: Plants build their leaves from carbon dioxide, water and light. Where does the carbon dioxide come from?

big_questions.q: Is it fair for one animal to eat another?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to the forest if there were no hunters at all? What if there were no vultures?

big_questions.q: Why does breathing slowly make you feel calm?
big_questions.hint: Try it. Breathe in for four counts, out for six. What changes in your body?

big_questions.q: Could an animal live on a planet with no oxygen at all?
big_questions.hint: In 2020, scientists found a tiny animal that lives inside fish muscle and does not use oxygen at all. Some bacteria on Earth also live with no oxygen. How might they get energy?

big_questions.q: Why did different animals end up with lungs, gills or breathing skin, instead of all having the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each one lives: dry land, water or damp soil.

story.title: The Fish in the Palm Tree
story.note: Tranquebar (now Tharangambadi, in Tamil Nadu) was a Danish trading town. A Danish officer, Lieutenant Daldorff, really did report in the 1790s that he saw a climbing perch high on a palm there, and his report was published in London in 1797. Selvi, her grandmother, the kite and everything the officer says and does in the story are imagined. The science of how the fish breathes is real.
text: The summer the tank dried, Selvi learned to hear fish breathing.

She was nine. She lived in Tranquebar, a town by the sea where the Danish ships came in, and where the old Danish fort stood on the sand. Behind her house was the village tank, a square pond with stone steps going down. In March it was full of water lilies. By May it was a brown puddle. By June it was cracked mud, hard as a roof tile.

Every evening her grandmother, Paati, took a short digging stick and went down the steps. Selvi followed with a clay pot. Paati knelt on the cracked mud and tapped it, the way you tap a coconut to hear if it is ripe. Where it sounded soft, she dug. And there, a hand deep in the mud, there were fish.

They were small and greenish, as long as Selvi's hand, with spiny fins and a dark spot near the tail. They were alive. They had been living in that mud for days, with no water at all. Paati dropped them into the pot with a fistful of wet mud and some wet leaves, and nothing else.
'You will kill them,' Selvi said the first time. 'Fish need water.'
'Not these,' said Paati. 'Put your ear to the pot.'
Selvi did. At first she heard nothing. Then, very softly, she heard it. A little click. A tiny wet gulp. Then another.
'They are breathing,' said Paati. 'They drink the air, like you and me. Just keep them damp. If they dry out, they die. If they stay damp, they live.'
Selvi did not understand it. She just remembered it, the way you remember a song.
That was the summer the Danish officer came walking through the palms.

He was a tall man with a red face and a notebook. The children called him the leaf man, because he picked up leaves, beetles, shells and stones, and wrote about every one. The grown-ups said he was a lieutenant at the fort. He spoke a little Tamil, badly and politely. Mostly he pointed.

One afternoon, after the first thunderstorm of the year, Selvi was sitting under the palmyra palms near the tank. The air smelled of wet dust. Above her, a black kite was circling. They dipped low over the puddles in the tank, came up with something silver in their claws, and flapped heavily to the top of the nearest palm. There they sat, tearing at their catch. Then a crow came. The kite and the crow screamed at each other. Something fell out of the kite's claws and tumbled down into the rough, cracked bark of the trunk.
Selvi stood up to look. Just then the leaf man came round the corner.

He saw them at once. A fish, wriggling in a cleft of the palm bark, as high as a man's shoulder. Their spiny gill covers were hooked into the bark. Their tail was flicking. They looked exactly as though they were climbing up.

The leaf man made a sound Selvi had never heard a grown man make. It was half a gasp and half a laugh. He took out his notebook. He looked at the fish, then wrote, then looked again. He measured the height with his hand. 'Climbing!' he said in his own language, and then in Tamil, 'They go up! The fish goes up the tree!'
Selvi opened her mouth to tell him about the kite. But he was talking fast, to himself, and he did not look at her.

He lifted the fish carefully from the bark. He looked worried now. He held the fish out in the bright, dry air and shook his head. 'They will die,' he said. 'No water. They will die.' He reached into his bag for a glass jar, the kind he kept beetles in, full of strong-smelling spirit. That was what he did with things he found. He kept them dead and still, so he could study them later.
And Selvi understood, all at once, what Paati had been telling her all summer.

'No,' she said. 'Wait.' She ran to her house and came back with the clay pot, the one with wet mud and wet leaves at the bottom. She held it out. He looked at her, then at the pot. Then, slowly, he put the fish in.

Selvi sprinkled water from her hands over the leaves. She did not fill the pot. The fish lay still, then wriggled down into the wet leaves. Then they came up and opened their mouth at the top of the pot, and took a gulp of air. Click. Then another.
The leaf man knelt down in the dust. He put his ear to the pot, the way Selvi had done.
'They breathe the air,' Selvi said in Tamil, slowly, so he would understand. 'Not only water. Keep them damp, and they live. Paati finds them in the dry tank every day.'

He listened for a long time. Then he looked up at the top of the palm, where the kite had gone. Selvi pointed at the sky, flapped her arms like a kite, opened her fingers and let an invisible fish drop. He watched her. She could not tell if he believed her.

He kept the fish alive in the pot for six days. Every evening Selvi came to sprinkle them, and every evening they gulped their little gulps of air. He drew them many times. He wrote pages and pages. Then the rains came properly, and the tank began to fill, and Selvi carried the pot down the stone steps and tipped the fish into the brown water.
They sank. Then they rose. At the surface, they took one more bubble of air, and was gone.

Years later, Selvi heard that the leaf man had sent his writing across the sea, to scientists in London. Later still, a scientist in France gave the fish the name Anabas, which means the one that climbs. Nobody wrote down a girl, a pot of wet mud, or a kite.
Selvi did not mind very much. On summer evenings, she still went down the steps of the dry tank with a digging stick, and knelt, and tapped, and listened for the click.
story.epiphany: The climbing perch was alive in the palm tree because they breathe air as well as water. As long as their body stays damp, they can live out of water for hours. So the fish did not have to climb to get up there. A bird could have dropped them, and they would still be alive.
ask: Why did Paati keep the fish in wet mud and wet leaves, and not in a pot full of water?
The leaf man thought the fish would die in air. Why do most fish die in air?
What did Selvi see that the leaf man did not? Why do you think he did not write it down?
How could you test whether a fish really climbs trees, or is dropped by birds?

games.title: Lungs, Gills or Skin?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

How do they find food? Pit viper: sensing heat

rules: Cut out the animal cards and the bonus cards. Shuffle the animal cards and put them face down.
Lay the four breathing mats in a row: LUNGS, GILLS, SKIN and AIR PIPES.
On your turn, take the top card and read the animal's name.
Put it on the mat that shows how they breathe, and say one reason. Some animals use two ways. Then put the card between two mats.
A right mat with a good reason wins one breath token. If someone thinks it is wrong, check the answer list together.
After every fifth card, turn over a bonus card. The first player to act out how that animal finds food wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.
games.context: Lungs, Gills or Skin? is a card game. You sort animals by how they breathe, and act out how some of them find food.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the four mats. 2. Shuffle the animal cards. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Almost every animal needs oxygen. But they get it in different ways: lungs, gills, damp skin, or tiny air pipes. Let's sort animals by how they breathe.
flow.kid: Lay out the four mats. Mix up the animal cards. Animals need oxygen. How does each one get it?

flow.do: Play the card 'Frog' together as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card: frog. Where does it go? Careful, this one is tricky.
flow.kid: Practice card: frog. Which mat? It might be two!

check.q: Practice card: frog. Where does it go?
options: Between LUNGS and SKIN
GILLS only
AIR PIPES
check.why: A grown frog breathes with lungs, and also through their thin, damp skin. That's why frogs stay near water. Picking 'gills' is half right for a young frog: a tadpole has gills. Once they grow up, most frogs breathe with lungs and skin.

flow.context: This is a practice round in Lungs, Gills or Skin? You decide where the frog card goes.

flow.do: Take turns until all cards are played. After every fifth card, turn over a bonus card. Use the answer list in the parent note when anyone disagrees.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the animal, put it on a mat, and give one reason. Every fifth card, we act out how an animal finds food.
flow.kid: Take a card. Put it on a mat. Say why. Every fifth card, act out a bonus card!
flow.parent: Answers. Lungs: cow, Ganges river dolphin, crow, python, elephant, sea turtle, bar-headed goose, bat, human baby, whale. Gills: rohu fish, tadpole, crab, prawn, shark, goldfish. Skin: earthworm, lungless salamander. Two ways: frog (lungs and skin), mudskipper (gills and skin), climbing perch (gills and a labyrinth organ that takes oxygen from air). Air pipes: grasshopper, butterfly, ant.

check.q: Card: Ganges river dolphin. They live in water all their life. Where does the card go?
options: LUNGS
GILLS
SKIN
check.why: Dolphins breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole. They come up every minute or two. Picking 'gills' usually means thinking that everything living in water breathes water. Living in water is not the same as breathing water.

flow.context: This is the main part of Lungs, Gills or Skin? You take turns sorting animal cards.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then each player names one animal from the game that surprised them.
flow.say: Let's count tokens. Which animal surprised you most?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Which animal surprised you most? Why?
flow.think: Can you think of an animal that breathes in a way none of our mats show?
flow.context: This is the end of Lungs, Gills or Skin? You count the tokens and talk about surprises.

games.title: Bat and Moth
games.players: 3 or more players, in a cleared room

printables.title: Role cards
items: TREE (stands still, says 'Tree!' if the bat comes close)

rules: Clear a space in a room. Its walls, or a ring of chairs and cushions, are the cave wall.
One player is the bat and wears a blindfold. One is the moth. Any other players are trees, who stand still inside the space.
The bat calls 'Bat!'. The moth must answer 'Moth!' straight away. Trees answer 'Tree!' if the bat is within two steps of them.
The moth's answer stands for the echo a real bat hears. The bat follows the answers to find and tag the moth, without touching a tree.
Time each round. Swap roles. The fastest bat wins.
games.context: Bat and Moth is a blindfold game. It shows how bats find insects in the dark by echolocation.

setup.art: A cleared living room ringed with chairs and cushions, one blindfolded child in the middle with arms out, another child crouching a few steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Clear a space. The bat wears a blindfold.

setup.art: The blindfolded child calling out, with speech bubble 'Bat!', and the moth answering 'Moth!'.
setup.caption: 2. The bat calls. The moth answers.
