setup.caption: 3. The bat follows the answers and tags the moth.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space and ring it with chairs or cushions. 2. Hand out the role cards. 3. Tie the blindfold on the bat.
flow.say: Bats hunt moths at night. Many bats can see, but in the dark they mostly listen. They make very high sounds and listen for the echo. Our bat will shout 'Bat!' and listen for 'Moth!'.
flow.kid: Clear a space. The bat wears a blindfold. The bat calls 'Bat!'. The moth must answer 'Moth!'.
flow.parent: Clear the floor of anything sharp or breakable. Walk beside the bat to keep them safe. Bats are not blind. Many see well, but they use sound in the dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bat and Moth. You set up a game that shows how bats hunt with echoes.

flow.do: Play rounds of about a minute each. Time each round. Swap roles so everyone is the bat once.
flow.say: Bat, call as often as you like. Moth, you must answer every time. Trees, warn the bat if they come close.
flow.kid: Bat: call and listen. Moth: always answer. Trees: say 'Tree!' if the bat comes near.

check.q: In Bat and Moth, the blindfolded bat found the moth by listening. What does a real bat listen for?
options: Echoes of their own high sounds bouncing off insects
The flap of the moth's wings only
Nothing, they smell the moth
check.why: Real bats send out sounds too high for us to hear. The sounds bounce off insects and come back as echoes. That's echolocation. Picking 'wing flaps' is not silly: some bats do also listen for the sounds prey makes. But mostly they use their own echoes.

flow.context: This is the main part of Bat and Moth. You play rounds, taking turns as the bat.

flow.do: Talk about how it felt to find food by sound.
flow.say: How did it feel to be the bat? Did it get easier with practice? Ganges river dolphins hunt fish in muddy water the same way, with clicks.
flow.kid: Was it hard to be the bat? Did it get easier? River dolphins hunt like this in muddy water.
flow.think: Moths have ears too. What might a clever moth do when they hear a bat coming?
flow.context: This is the end of Bat and Moth. You talk about finding food by sound.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: the basics

items.p: A rohu is a river fish who never leaves the water. Does a rohu need oxygen?
opts: Yes. Every cell in their body needs oxygen, and their gills take it out of the water
No. Fish live in water, so they do not need oxygen
Only when they jump out of the water
items.why: Many people think fish do not breathe. But water has oxygen dissolved in it, and a fish's gills take it out. A rohu's cells use that oxygen to get energy from food, just as yours do.

items.p: Fish take oxygen out of water with their ____.
items.why: Gills are the feathery red parts under the flaps on a fish's head. Water flows over them and they take oxygen out.

items.p: Sort these animals by how they mainly breathe.
items.a: see items
items.why: Land animals like cows and crows use lungs. So do dolphins, even though they live in water. Fish and crabs use gills. Earthworms and lungless salamanders breathe only through their skin.

items.p: You breathe on a cold steel tumbler and a mist appears. This shows your breath has water in it.
items.why: True. Your breath is warm and carries water as an invisible gas. On the cold steel it cools and turns back into tiny drops, which you see as mist.
items.context: In Breath on a Steel Tumbler, you breathed on cold steel, a mirror and a tissue, and watched what your breath did.

items.p: Predict. You count your breaths for one minute sitting still. Then you run up two floors of stairs and count again. What will you find?
opts: More breaths after the stairs, because working muscles need more oxygen
Fewer breaths, because you are tired
The same number, because lungs always work at one speed
items.why: Climbing stairs makes your leg muscles work hard. Working muscles use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, so you breathe faster. A strong answer gives the reason, not just the guess.
items.context: In the Breath Count experiment, you counted your breaths for one minute sitting still, then just after jumping.

items.p: In the Limewater Test, the glass with your breath turned milky. The glass with room air stayed clear. Kavya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'The milky colour just comes from bubbles.' How does the room-air glass show she is wrong?
items.a: Both glasses got bubbles, but only the breath glass went milky. So the bubbles alone did not do it. Something in breath, carbon dioxide, made the limewater milky.
items.why: The room-air glass is the comparison. Everything was the same except the kind of air, so the difference must come from the air.
items.context: In the Limewater Test, you bubbled your breath into one glass of limewater and pushed room air from a squeezed bottle into another glass.

items.p: Why do frogs need to stay near water? Use the word skin in your answer.
items.a: Frogs breathe partly through their skin. Their skin must stay damp for oxygen to pass through. If they go too far from water, their skin dries out and they cannot breathe well.
items.why: Skin breathing only works when the skin is thin and damp.

items.p: Why is a fish's gill made of many thin, frilly threads?
opts: To give lots of surface for oxygen to pass through
To help them swim faster
To keep sand out of their eyes
items.why: More surface lets more oxygen in at once. Remember the towel test: the frilly towel dried much faster than the crumpled one. Picking 'swim faster' mixes gills up with fins.
items.context: In the gill shape test, you hung up a crumpled wet towel and a frilly wet towel to see which dried first.

items.p: Draw a fish. Draw arrows to show where water goes in and where it goes out. Colour the gills.
items.a: An arrow into the mouth, an arrow out from under the gill cover, and red gills under the cover.
items.why: Water goes in at the mouth, flows over the gills, and goes out under the gill cover.
items.art: The outline of a fish side-on, with a dotted line where the gill cover is.

items.p: Match each animal to how they mainly find food.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal relies most on the sense that suits their life. Bats hunt in the dark by echoes. Dogs follow smells. Eagles see far. Owls hear mice in the dark. Pit vipers feel the warmth of a mouse.

items.p: A dolphin lives in the sea all the time. Why does a dolphin keep coming up to the surface?
opts: They breathe air with lungs, through the blowhole on top of their head
They come up to look for birds
Their gills need fresh air to dry them
items.why: Dolphins are mammals, not fish. They have lungs, not gills, so they must come up to breathe air. Picking 'gills' is a common mix-up, because dolphins live in water like fish.

items.p: Ants on a sugar trail walk in a line. Why?
opts: They follow a smell trail left by the ants who found the food
They can see the sugar from far away
The wind blows them in a line
items.why: An ant who finds food leaves a smell trail on the way home. Other ants follow it with their antennae, so they walk in a line. Picking 'see the sugar' is a natural guess, but ants find food mostly by smell.
items.context: In Ant Detectives, you put out sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path and watched the ants come.

items.p: Bats are blind.
items.why: False. All bats can see, and many see well. Many bats that hunt insects at night also use echolocation: they make high sounds and listen for the echoes. 'As blind as a bat' is an old saying, not a fact.

items.p: In the Mouth Tools Buffet, you tried kitchen tools as animal mouths. A flamingo's beak works like a sieve. A cow has wide, flat teeth. What does each mouth tell you about how that animal gets food?
items.a: The flamingo's sieve beak lets water out and keeps tiny shrimps and algae in, so she is a filter feeder. The cow's flat teeth grind grass, so she is a grazer who chews plants for hours.
items.why: An animal's mouth fits the way they get food. A strong answer links each mouth shape to the food and how it is eaten.
items.context: In the Mouth Tools Buffet, you pretended kitchen tools were animal mouths and found which tool was best for which food.

items.p: Three friends argue about which way of breathing is best.

views.says: Lungs are best. Air has about 30 times more oxygen than water.
Gills are best for a fish. Lungs would fill with water and be useless in a river.
Having two ways is best, like a frog. Lungs work on land, and damp skin works in the pond.

items.ask: Which way do you think is best? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, for example that air holds much more oxygen. It then admits a fair point from another side, for example that a breathing part is best only where the animal lives. It may say that all three are thin, damp and close to blood.
items.why: There is no single winner. Each breathing part suits the place the animal lives. Lungs suit air, gills suit water, and a frog's skin helps in both, as long as it stays damp.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: think further

items.p: A fish has gills full of blood. Out of water, they usually die, even though air has more oxygen than water. Why?
opts: Their soft gill threads stick together and dry out, so there is too little surface
Air is poisonous to fish
Fish get cold in air
items.why: Out of water, the thin gill threads collapse and stick together, like a wet paintbrush pulled out of a jar. Then there is too little damp surface for oxygen to pass through. Picking 'poisonous' is a common idea, but air is not poisonous. Some fish, like the climbing perch, can even breathe it.

items.p: Your diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under your lungs. What does it do when you breathe in?
opts: It pulls down, making space, and air rushes into the lungs
It pushes air up into the nose
It squeezes the heart
items.why: When the diaphragm pulls down, there is more space in the chest, and air flows in to fill it. That's what the bottle lung showed. Picking 'pushes air up' is what happens when you breathe out, not in.
items.context: In Make a Bottle Lung, you pulled the stretchy balloon at the bottom of a bottle and watched the balloon inside fill.

items.p: A grasshopper has no lungs. How does air reach the muscles in the grasshopper's legs?
items.a: Air goes in through tiny holes along the grasshopper's sides, called spiracles. It travels down thin air pipes that branch again and again until they reach every muscle. So air goes straight to the cells.
items.why: In insects, air pipes carry oxygen right to the cells, so their blood does not have to carry much oxygen.

items.p: The climbing perch can live out of water for hours. What lets them do this?
opts: A labyrinth organ above their gills that takes oxygen from air
They hold their breath for a very long time
They don't need oxygen when they're dry
items.why: The climbing perch has a folded, maze-like labyrinth organ above their gills. They gulp air and take oxygen from it, as long as their body stays damp. Picking 'hold their breath' would only work for a short time.

items.p: Look at the ant chart. Most ants went to the sugar and almost none to the salt. Predict: if you put out jaggery instead of salt, what would you expect?
opts: Many ants, like on the sugar, because jaggery is mostly sugar too
No ants, because jaggery is brown
Exactly one ant, like on the salt
items.why: Jaggery is mostly sugar, which is energy food for ants. So it should get many ants, like the sugar. Picking 'brown' would matter only if ants found food by colour, but they find it mostly by smell.

chart.title: Made-up results: ants on each bait after 30 minutes

items.context: In Ant Detectives, you counted the ants on sugar, biscuit and salt after 30 minutes.

items.p: A Ganges river dolphin is nearly blind and lives in muddy water. How do they find fish?
opts: They send out clicks and listen to the echoes
They see them with big eyes
They wait for fish to jump into their mouth
items.why: The Ganges river dolphin uses echolocation. They send out clicks, and the echoes tell them where fish are. Their eyes are tiny because seeing doesn't help much in muddy water.

items.p: A mosquito can find you in the dark by sensing the carbon dioxide you breathe out.
items.why: True. Mosquitoes sense carbon dioxide from a distance, then follow warmth and smell close up.

items.p: Predict the order, from fewest breaths a minute to most: elephant, child, mouse.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Big animals usually breathe more slowly than small ones. An elephant takes only a few breaths a minute. A child takes about 20. A mouse takes more than 100.

items.p: A cheetah hunts by chasing. A crocodile hunts by waiting. Which do you think needs to breathe faster while hunting? Why?
items.a: The cheetah. Chasing at high speed uses a lot of muscle, and working muscles need a lot of oxygen. A crocodile waiting still uses very little oxygen.
items.why: Breathing rate goes with how hard the muscles are working.

items.p: Label the parts on the drawing of the breathing system: nose, windpipe, lungs, diaphragm.
items.why: Air goes in through the nose, down the windpipe, into the lungs. The diaphragm under the lungs pulls down to bring air in.
items.art: An outline of a child's upper body with the breathing system drawn in and four blank label lines.

items.p: Match each way of getting food to an animal that uses it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal's body fits their way of eating: flat teeth for grazing, long legs for chasing, stillness for waiting, a sieve beak for filtering, a web for trapping, and a strong stomach for scavenging.

items.p: Earthworms often lie on wet roads after heavy rain. People explain this in different ways.

views.who: Anjali, who grows plants on her terrace
views.says: They come up so they don't drown in the wet soil.
Worms can live for a long time in water that has oxygen in it. They come up because wet ground lets them travel far without drying out.
Rain drumming on the ground feels like a mole digging, so they escape.

items.ask: Pick the idea you think is most likely. Give your reason. Then say how you could test one of the ideas.
items.a: A strong answer picks one idea and gives evidence, for example that worms breathe through damp skin. It plans a fair test, for example drumming on damp soil with no rain to see if worms come up. It also says what is good about another idea.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this, and more than one reason may be true. Testing one idea at a time is how they find out.

items.p: In the story 'The Fish in the Palm Tree', Selvi's grandmother keeps climbing perch in a pot of wet mud and wet leaves. The fish live for days. Why must the mud stay damp, even for a fish that breathes air?
items.a: The climbing perch gulps air, but oxygen still has to pass through a thin, damp surface into the blood. If the fish dries out, their gills and labyrinth organ stop working, and they cannot breathe.
items.why: Every breathing surface must be damp, because oxygen has to dissolve in water before it can pass into blood.

items.p: Why do mammals like dolphins and whales store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles?
opts: So they can stay underwater longer while hunting
To make them float
To keep their skin wet
items.why: Diving animals can't breathe underwater. Extra stored oxygen lets them hunt for longer before coming up. Some deep-diving whales stay down for over an hour.

items.p: A crab who walks on the beach breathes with gills.
items.why: True. Crabs breathe with gills, even on land. They keep their gills damp inside a covered space on each side of their body. If the gills dry out, the crab cannot breathe.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: big thinking

items.p: Lungs, gills and frog skin look very different. Write three things they all have in common.
items.a: They are thin. They are damp. They have lots of surface, and blood flows just underneath.
items.why: All breathing surfaces work the same way: oxygen passes through a thin, wet wall into blood.

items.p: Water holds about 30 times less oxygen than air. What would you expect a fish to do in warm, still water with even less oxygen?
opts: Move their gill covers faster, or come to the surface
Stop breathing to save oxygen
Sleep until the water gets better
items.why: With less oxygen in the water, a fish must push more water over their gills, so they pump faster. Some fish come to the surface, where the water has a little more oxygen. Picking 'stop breathing' would be fatal. Every cell needs a steady supply.

items.p: The oxygen you breathe was put into the air by plants and tiny sea algae.
items.why: True. Plants and algae make oxygen when they make food from sunlight. Scientists think about half of the oxygen made each year comes from tiny algae in the sea.

items.p: Scientists have argued about where lungs came from.

views.says: Lungs came from the swim bladder, the air bag that many fish use to float.
Lungs came first, in early fish that gulped air in warm, muddy water. The swim bladder came later, from those lungs.

items.ask: Which idea do you find more likely? What evidence would help you decide? Then say why the other idea once seemed sensible.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and names evidence, for example that some old kinds of fish alive today, like lungfish, have lungs and gulp air in muddy water. It explains why Darwin's idea seemed sensible: both are air bags in the body. It says that new evidence can change scientists' minds.
items.why: Darwin's idea was reasonable for his time. Studies of living fish and fossils now point the other way. Science changes when evidence changes.

items.p: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas, where each breath of air holds much less oxygen. Predict two things about their bodies that would help them get enough oxygen.
items.a: For example: big lungs that take in a lot of air, blood that picks up oxygen very easily, a strong heart that pumps fast, or breathing deeply. Real bar-headed geese have all of these.
items.why: When each breath carries less oxygen, an animal needs to take in more air or pick up oxygen better.

items.p: Some bats eat moths. Many moths can hear bat sounds. What might a moth do when they hear a bat?
opts: Dive, dodge or drop to the ground
Fly straight towards the bat
Sing back louder
items.why: Many moths dodge or drop when they hear a bat's high sounds. Some even make clicks that confuse bats. Predator and prey keep changing each other over a very long time.

items.p: A Cuvier's beaked whale once stayed under water for 222 minutes, nearly 4 hours. Which is the best reason a whale can do this?
opts: They store a lot of oxygen in their blood and muscles, and their heart slows down while diving
They have gills hidden behind their flippers
They breathe through their skin under water
items.why: Whales have lungs and no gills, so they cannot breathe under water. Their blood and muscles hold extra oxygen, and their body uses it slowly while diving. Picking 'gills' is the old idea that whales are fish.

items.p: Plants make oxygen, so plants never need to take oxygen in.
items.why: False. Plant cells also use oxygen to get energy from their food, day and night. In sunlight, plants make much more oxygen than they use. At night, they only take it in.

items.p: The tiny energy parts in your cells, called mitochondria, use oxygen. Where did scientists find they came from?
opts: Tiny bacteria that moved into bigger cells long ago
From eating fish
From the air
items.why: Lynn Margulis argued in 1967 that mitochondria came from bacteria living inside bigger cells. DNA tests later showed she was right. So the parts of your cells that use oxygen were once bacteria.

items.p: Kamala Sohonie was the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, in 1939. She found that plant cells have cytochrome c, a substance animal cells also use in breathing. What does her discovery tell us about plants and animals?
items.a: Plants and animals use some of the same parts to breathe. Their cells work in a similar way, even though they look so different.
items.why: Plants and animals use some of the same chemicals to use oxygen. This makes sense, because all living things share one ancestor.

items.p: Imagine the bottom of a dark, muddy river. Sort these senses: which would work well there, and which would hardly work?
items: spotting prey from far away by sight
items.a: see items
items.why: Light hardly reaches muddy water, so eyes help little. Smell, taste, touch, echoes and electricity all work in the dark. The Ganges river dolphin uses echoes, and catfish taste the water with their whiskers.

items.p: Design a breathing part for an animal that lives in thick mud with almost no oxygen. Draw it and explain why it would work.
items.a: For example: a long tube like a snorkel reaching up to the air, or skin with many folds to give lots of surface, or a mouth that gulps air like the climbing perch.
items.why: Good designs give lots of surface, stay damp, or reach air.

items.p: Karthik, a boy in Class 4, says, 'We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide instead.' His sister Divya has done the Limewater Test and read about breath. What should Divya tell him?
opts: Breathed-out air still has a lot of oxygen. It also has much more carbon dioxide than room air
He is completely right
We breathe out only water
items.why: Room air has about 21 parts in 100 oxygen, and breathed-out air still has about 16. Your body takes only a small part of the oxygen in each breath. Breath also carries about 100 times more carbon dioxide than room air.
items.context: In the Limewater Test, you bubbled your breath into one glass of limewater and pushed room air from a squeezed bottle into another glass.

items.p: In the limewater test, your breath turned the water milky. The carbon dioxide in your breath was made in your cells. Where did the carbon in it come from?
items.a: From my food. My cells used oxygen to break down the food for energy. The carbon in the food came out as carbon dioxide, and I breathed it out.
items.why: Respiration turns food and oxygen into energy, carbon dioxide and water. So part of every meal leaves the body in the breath.
items.context: In the Limewater Test, you bubbled your breath into limewater and it turned milky.

items.p: Match each animal's problem to the body part or trick that solves it.
pairs: climbing perch, in warm water with little oxygen
a labyrinth organ to breathe gulped air
Cuvier's beaked whale, with no air for hours
oxygen stored in blood and muscles
thin, damp skin that takes in oxygen
air pipes that reach every part of the body
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each body solves the same problem, getting oxygen to the cells, in a way that fits where the animal lives.

experiments.title: Breath Count: before and after jumping
experiments.question: Do we breathe faster after exercise? How much faster?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many breaths do you take in one minute while sitting still? Will the number go up, go down or stay the same after one minute of jumping? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, count in the same way every time: sit in the same chair, and count for the same time. Only one thing changes: resting or just after jumping. Count 3 times for each, because one count can be a fluke.

materials.item: a phone, clock or watch that can time one minute
a pencil and the results table
a chair
a grown-up or friend to count with you

experiments.safety: Jump on a flat, non-slippery floor, away from furniture. Stop if you feel dizzy or unwell. Children with asthma can skip the jumping and count a grown-up's breaths instead.

schedule.what: Guess. Count breaths sitting still, 3 times. Jump for one minute. Count again. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars: one for resting, one for after jumping. Then write a claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment you count your breaths in one minute, sitting still and then just after jumping, to see if exercise changes breathing.

setup.art: A child sitting still on a chair, one hand resting on the chest, a grown-up holding a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still. Put a hand on your chest. Count your breaths for one minute.

setup.art: The same child jumping on the spot on a rug, arms up, a timer showing one minute.
setup.caption: 2. Jump on the spot for one minute.

setup.art: The child sitting again, panting, hand on chest, while the grown-up writes a number in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Sit down straight away. Count your breaths for one minute again.

flow.do: 1. Sit your child on a chair. 2. Ask them to guess how many breaths they take in one minute. 3. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Each time your chest goes up and down, that is one breath. How many breaths do you think you take in one minute, sitting still? And after jumping, will it be more or fewer?
flow.kid: One breath is one up and one down of your chest. How many breaths in a minute? Guess a number. Write it down.

ask.q: What do you think will happen after jumping? Why?
good: More breaths, because I will be puffed out.
Faster, because my body needs more air when I move.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Breath Count experiment. You guess how many breaths you take in one minute.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still for one minute first, to settle. 2. They put one hand flat on their chest. 3. Start the timer. They count each rise of the chest, quietly. 4. Stop at one minute and write the number. 5. Rest one minute and repeat, until there are 3 counts.
flow.say: Put your hand on your chest. Breathe normally, don't try to change it. I'll say go, and you count each time your chest rises. Ready? Go.
flow.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your chest. Breathe normally. Count each time your chest goes up. Stop when the minute ends. Write the number. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Most children of 6 to 10 take about 18 to 25 breaths a minute at rest. It's fine if the first count is odd, because counting your own breath changes it a little. That's why we count three times. If counting is hard, the grown-up can watch and count instead.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.context: This is the step where you count your breaths while sitting still, three times.

flow.do: 1. Your child jumps on the spot for one full minute. 2. The moment the minute ends, they sit down. 3. Start the timer straight away and count breaths for one minute. 4. Write the number. 5. Rest three minutes, then repeat twice more.
flow.say: Now jump on the spot for one whole minute, as fast as is comfortable. The second I say stop, sit down, hand on chest, and we count straight away.
flow.kid: Jump on the spot for one minute. Then sit down fast. Hand on your chest. Count your breaths for one minute. Write the number.
flow.parent: Watch for dizziness and let your child stop early if needed. Count straight away, because breathing slows back down within a few minutes. Wait until breathing feels normal before the next jump.
flow.context: This is the step where you jump for one minute and then count your breaths again.

flow.do: 1. Find the middle value of each set of three counts: put them in order and take the middle one. 2. Draw two bars, one for sitting still and one for after jumping.
flow.say: Let's turn our numbers into a picture. One bar for resting. One bar for after jumping. The taller the bar, the more breaths in a minute.
flow.kid: Put your three numbers in order. The middle one is your middle value. Draw a bar for resting. Draw a bar for after jumping.

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Yours will be different.

check.q: In the breath count chart, the bar for after jumping is taller. What does that tell us?
options: We breathe more times in a minute after jumping
We breathe fewer times after jumping
Jumping makes us taller
check.why: Each bar shows how many breaths were counted in one minute. A taller bar means more breaths. Picking 'fewer' usually means the bars were read the wrong way round. Look at the numbers on the side of the chart to check.

flow.context: This is the step where you turn your breath counts into a bar chart.

flow.do: Help your child say or write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's explain what we found, like a scientist. First, what do you think? That's your claim. Then, what did you see? That's your evidence. Then, why? That's your reasoning.
flow.kid: Say what you found. Then say what numbers showed it. Then say why it happened.

ask.q: Claim: what happens to breathing after exercise?
good: We breathe faster after exercise.

ask.q: Evidence: what did your numbers show?
good: Sitting still I took 20 breaths a minute. After jumping I took 40.

ask.q: Reasoning: why?
good: My leg muscles were working hard. They needed more oxygen, so I breathed faster to get more air in.
My muscles made more carbon dioxide, and I had to breathe it out.

check.q: Why do we breathe faster after jumping?
options: Our muscles need more oxygen to get energy from food
Our lungs get tired and slow down
Jumping shakes extra air into our nose
check.why: Working muscles do more respiration, which means they use more oxygen to unlock energy from food. Breathing faster brings that oxygen in and takes the extra carbon dioxide out. Picking 'lungs get tired' mixes up breathing with tiredness. Picking 'shakes air in' means thinking air gets in by itself, but our muscles pull it in.

flow.think: A cheetah after a chase pants very hard. A sleeping python breathes only a few times a minute. Why might that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Breath Count experiment. You explain what you found, using claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: The Limewater Test: what is in your breath?
experiments.question: Is the air we breathe out different from the air in the room?
experiments.predict: Guess first. We will bubble your breath into one glass of limewater, and room air into another. Will they look the same at the end? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both glasses get the same amount of limewater and the same kind of straw, and air is bubbled in for the same time. Only the kind of air changes: your breath, or room air pushed out of an empty plastic bottle.

materials.item: edible chuna, the white lime paste sold at paan shops
two clear glasses
two drinking straws
an empty plastic bottle, a small ball of atta dough (or a bicycle pump, if you have one)
a jug with about 1 litre of tap water
a phone or clock to time one minute

experiments.safety: Chuna can burn skin and eyes. Only a grown-up handles it. Never taste chuna or limewater, and never drink it. If any splashes in an eye, rinse the eye with plenty of clean water for several minutes and call a doctor. Blow out through the straw only, never suck. Wash hands afterwards, and pour the limewater down the sink with plenty of tap water.

schedule.what: A grown-up stirs one teaspoon of chuna into about a litre of water and leaves it overnight to settle.
Pour off the clear limewater. Bubble breath into one glass and room air from a squeezed bottle into the other. Compare, and talk about where the carbon dioxide came from.

experiments.record: Draw the two glasses after 2 minutes. Write which one turned milky first. Then write your claim, evidence and reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use clear limewater, which turns milky when carbon dioxide bubbles through it. If you did the milky breath test in the Heart, blood and breath unit, this is the same test with a new question. There you found that breath is different from room air. Here you also ask where the carbon dioxide in your breath came from. You find out whether breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide than room air, and where that carbon dioxide comes from.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a spoon of white chuna paste into a steel jug of water, then the jug resting overnight with white powder settled at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up mixes chuna in water. Leave it overnight.

setup.art: Two glasses of clear limewater side by side: a child blowing gently through a straw into one, and a grown-up squeezing an empty plastic bottle so room air bubbles through a straw into the other.
setup.caption: 2. Blow breath into one glass. Squeeze room air from a bottle into the other.

setup.art: The same two glasses after two minutes: the breath glass cloudy white like milk, the room-air glass still almost clear.
setup.caption: 3. Compare. Which one turned milky?

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Stir one level teaspoon of edible chuna into about 1 litre of tap water in a jug. 2. Cover the jug with a plate, so room air does not reach it. Leave it overnight, out of children's reach.
flow.say: This is chuna, the lime paste people put on paan leaves. Mixed with water, it makes limewater. Limewater changes when carbon dioxide gets into it. Chuna can burn skin and eyes, so only I touch it.
flow.kid: Today a grown-up mixes chuna in water. Chuna can burn your skin, so don't touch it. Tomorrow you will use the clear water.
flow.wait: Leave the jug overnight so the white powder settles.
flow.parent: Edible chuna is calcium hydroxide, also called slaked lime. It is caustic, so keep it away from eyes and wash your hands after touching it. When it settles, the clear water on top is limewater, the same liquid used in school labs. If the water is still cloudy in the morning, leave it a few more hours.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Limewater Test. A grown-up makes limewater from chuna, the lime paste sold at paan shops.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Gently pour the clear water from the top of the jug into two glasses, half full each. Leave the white powder behind. 2. Put a straw in glass 1. 3. Push a second straw into the neck of the empty bottle, and press atta dough round it so no air leaks. This bottle will push room air into glass 2.
flow.say: Look, both glasses are clear. Carbon dioxide turns this water milky. Which kind of air do you think has more carbon dioxide: your breath, or the air in this room? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the two glasses. Both are clear. Guess. Which will turn milky: your breath or room air?

ask.q: Which glass do you think will turn milky first? Why?
good: The breath one, because we breathe out carbon dioxide.
The breath one, because our body puts used air out.

flow.context: This is the step where you pour the clear limewater into two glasses and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child blows gently out through the straw in glass 1 for one minute, breathing in through the nose. 2. At the same time, a grown-up puts the bottle's straw into glass 2 and squeezes the bottle, so room air bubbles out. Lift the straw out of the water before letting go, so the bottle refills with room air, not limewater. Do this about 20 times in the minute. 3. Check both glasses at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 2 minutes.
flow.say: Blow out gently through the straw, in slow bubbles. Breathe in through your nose, never through the straw. I'll squeeze room air from the bottle into the other glass at the same time.
flow.kid: Breathe in through your nose. Blow out gently through the straw. Never suck. Watch the bubbles. A grown-up squeezes air into the other glass.
flow.parent: The breath glass usually goes cloudy within 30 seconds to a minute. The room-air glass stays nearly clear, because room air has only a tiny bit of carbon dioxide. Stop at 2 minutes: if you keep blowing for many minutes, the milkiness can clear again. If your child sucks by mistake, rinse their mouth with plenty of water. A bicycle pump works instead of the bottle, if you have one.
flow.context: This is the step where you bubble your breath into one glass of limewater, and room air into the other.

flow.do: Compare the glasses and talk about claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you see? Which glass turned milky? Why do you think that happened? So which air had more carbon dioxide?
flow.kid: Which glass turned milky? Milky means carbon dioxide. Where did the carbon dioxide in your breath come from?

ask.q: Claim: is breathed-out air different from room air?
good: Yes. Breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide.

ask.q: Evidence?
good: The breath glass went milky in under a minute. The room-air glass stayed clear.

ask.q: Reasoning?
good: My cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide. My blood carries it to my lungs, and I breathe it out.

ask.q: Where do you think the carbon dioxide in your breath came from?
good: From my body.
My cells made it from the food I ate, when they used oxygen to get energy.
From my lunch.

check.q: The limewater with breath turned milky. The one with room air stayed clear. Why?
options: Breathed-out air has much more carbon dioxide than room air
Breathed-out air has no oxygen at all
Spit from the straw made it milky
check.why: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, and breathed-out air carries carbon dioxide made by your cells from food. Picking 'no oxygen at all' is a common mistake. Breathed-out air still has a lot of oxygen, just a bit less. Picking 'spit' is a good scientist's worry. But only a tiny drop of spit could get in, and the whole glass turned milky as the bubbles went through. Only carbon dioxide does that to limewater.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Limewater Test. You compare the two glasses and explain what happened.
flow.parent: Let your child guess first. Then explain: the milky colour is tiny bits of calcium carbonate, the same material as chalk and eggshell. It forms when carbon dioxide meets limewater. Your cells use oxygen to get energy from food. The carbon in the food comes out as carbon dioxide, and the blood carries it to the lungs. So part of every meal leaves the body in the breath. This is the idea behind the unit's deep truth.

experiments.title: Ant Detectives: which food do ants find first?
experiments.question: How do ants find food? Do they find some foods faster than others?
experiments.predict: Guess first. We will put out three baits: sugar, salt and a crumb of biscuit. Which will the first ant find? Which will have the most ants after 30 minutes? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Put the three baits the same size, the same distance from the ants' path, on the same kind of paper, at the same time. Only the food changes. Count the ants on each bait at 10, 20 and 30 minutes.

materials.item: three small squares of white paper or card
a pinch of sugar, a pinch of salt, a crumb of biscuit
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a phone or clock, and the results table

experiments.safety: Use common small black ants, not red ants or big biting ants. Watch, don't touch. Clean up the baits afterwards so ants don't come into the kitchen.

schedule.what: Find an ant path. Lay out three baits. Count ants every 10 minutes for 30 minutes. Watch how they find the food.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of ants at 30 minutes. Draw a map of the ant trail you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put out sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path, and count how many ants find each one. It shows how ants use smell to find food.

setup.art: Three small white paper squares on a kitchen floor near a wall, one with sugar, one with salt, one with a biscuit crumb, each the same distance from a line of small black ants.
setup.caption: 1. Put three baits the same distance from an ant path.

setup.art: A child with a magnifying glass crouched over the sugar square, with ants gathering on it and a timer beside.
setup.caption: 2. Count the ants on each bait every 10 minutes.

setup.art: A line of ants walking in single file from the sugar back to a crack in the wall, following an invisible dotted smell trail.
setup.caption: 3. Watch how the ants follow each other back home.

flow.do: 1. Find a line of small black ants: in the kitchen, on a window sill or on the balcony. 2. Put the three paper squares about one hand-length from the line, side by side, a hand-length apart. 3. Put the sugar, salt and biscuit crumb on them.
flow.say: Ants have no noses, but they smell with their feelers, the two thin antennae on their heads. Let's see if they can find our food. Which one do you think they'll find first?
flow.kid: Find a line of ants. Put three papers near it. Put sugar on one, salt on one, biscuit on one. Which will ants find first?

ask.q: How do you think an ant knows where food is?
good: They smell it.
They feel it with their feelers.
Other ants show them the way.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ant Detectives. You put three kinds of food near an ant path.
flow.parent: Most Indian homes have small ants somewhere. If you cannot see any, put a pinch of sugar on a paper near a window or balcony crack the day before. Ants usually find it within a day, and you can start the test where they come.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Watch quietly. Note which bait the first ant reaches, and how long it took. 3. At 10, 20 and 30 minutes, count the ants on each bait and write the numbers in the table. 4. In between, watch one ant leave the food and follow them.
flow.say: Look, one ant found the sugar. Watch what they do next. Do they go home? Do they touch other ants? Let's count every ten minutes.
flow.kid: Watch quietly. Which food did the first ant find? Count the ants on each paper every ten minutes. Follow one ant with your eyes.
flow.parent: Usually one scout ant finds the sugar or biscuit by smell, wanders back towards the nest, and soon a trail of ants arrives. The scout leaves a smell trail, called a pheromone trail, on the way home. Salt usually gets few or no ants. Results vary with the kind of ant, so whatever happens is real data.

chart.title: Made-up example: ants on each bait after 30 minutes
chart.note: Made-up numbers to show what a chart can look like. Your ants will be different.

flow.context: This is the step where you watch and count the ants on each bait for 30 minutes.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw, using claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: So, what do we think? How do ants find food? What did you see that tells you? And why do the other ants arrive in a line?
flow.kid: Say what you found. What numbers show it? Why did the ants walk in a line?

ask.q: Claim?
good: Ants find sweet food by smell, and they find sugar faster than salt.

ask.q: Evidence?
good: After 30 minutes there were 24 ants on the sugar and only 1 on the salt.
The ants walked in a line from the sugar to their nest.

ask.q: Reasoning?
good: Sugar is energy food. The first ant smelled it and left a smell trail home. The others followed the trail.

check.q: Ants arrived at the sugar in a long line. How did they know the way?
options: They followed a smell trail left by the first ant
They could see the sugar from far away
They heard the sugar
check.why: Ants that find food leave a trail of smell on the way back to the nest. Other ants follow it with their antennae. Most small ants see poorly, so picking 'see' is a good guess but not how they do it. Try this: rub a finger across the trail. Watch the ants get confused where the smell is wiped away.

flow.think: If you wipe your finger across the ant trail, what will the ants do? Try it gently and see.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ant Detectives. You explain how the ants found the food.

activities.title: Breath on a Steel Tumbler

materials.item: a steel tumbler or steel plate, at room temperature
a small mirror
a strip of tissue paper

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.
activities.record: Draw what you saw on the tumbler and the tissue. Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You breathe on steel, a mirror and a tissue, and notice what your breath does.

setup.art: A child breathing out slowly onto a shiny steel tumbler, a misty patch forming on it.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe out slowly onto a steel tumbler.

setup.art: The child holding a thin strip of tissue under the nose, the tissue fluttering outwards.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a tissue strip under your nose. Watch it move.

setup.art: The child with one hand on the chest and one on the belly, both rising, eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Put a hand on your chest and one on your belly. Feel them move.

flow.do: 1. Hold the steel tumbler close to your child's mouth. 2. Your child breathes out slowly onto it, three times. 3. Then onto the mirror. 4. Then they hold a tissue strip under their nose and breathe in and out.
flow.say: Breathe out slowly onto the steel. What appears? Now hold the tissue under your nose. What does it do when you breathe in? When you breathe out?
flow.kid: Breathe out on the steel. What do you see? Hold the tissue under your nose. Watch it move.

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: The steel goes misty.
Little drops of water appear.
The tissue blows away when I breathe out and comes closer when I breathe in.

ask.q: What do you wonder?
good: Where does the water come from?
Does a fish breathe like this?
What is in my breath?

flow.parent: The mist is water. Breath is warm and full of water vapour, a gas. On the cooler steel, the vapour condenses: it turns into tiny drops. If the steel does not mist on a very hot day, cool it under the tap for a minute and dry it. Don't explain more yet. The unit will answer the child's wonders.
flow.context: This is the first step of Breath on a Steel Tumbler. You breathe on steel and a tissue and notice what happens.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still, one hand on the chest and one on the belly. 2. They breathe normally for ten breaths and notice which hand moves. 3. Then they take three big slow breaths.
flow.say: Close your eyes. One hand on your chest, one on your belly. Just notice. Which hand moves? Now take a big slow breath in. Where does the air go?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. One hand on your chest. One hand on your belly. Breathe. Which hand moves? Now take a big, slow breath.

check.q: Your breath made the steel tumbler misty. What is the mist?
options: Tiny drops of water from your breath
Smoke from inside your body
Oxygen you can see
check.why: Your breath is warm and full of water vapour. When it touches cooler steel, the vapour turns into tiny drops, just like the drops on a cold glass of water. Picking 'smoke' means thinking breathing is like burning. That is partly a good idea, because cells do use oxygen to get energy from food, but there is no smoke. Oxygen has no colour, so you can never see it.

flow.think: You breathed out water. Where did that water come from? A fish lives in water. How does a fish breathe?
flow.context: This is the step where you feel your chest and belly move as you breathe.

activities.title: Make a Bottle Lung

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle, about 1 litre
two balloons
a rubber band
scissors or a cutter, for a grown-up
sticky tape

activities.safety: Only a grown-up cuts the bottle. Cover the cut edge with tape so it isn't sharp.
activities.record: Draw your bottle lung. Label the balloon lung, the windpipe and the diaphragm. Draw arrows showing which way air goes when you pull down.
activities.context: In this activity you build a model lung from a bottle and two balloons, to see how a sheet of muscle under the lungs pulls air in.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting the bottom off a clear plastic bottle, tape ready on the table.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom off a bottle.

setup.art: A balloon hanging inside the bottle from its neck, and a second balloon, knotted and cut, stretched over the open bottom like a drum.
setup.caption: 2. Hang one balloon inside. Stretch the other over the bottom.

setup.art: A child pulling the knot of the bottom balloon down, the balloon inside the bottle puffing up with air.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the bottom balloon down. Watch the lung fill.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts off the bottom third of the bottle and tapes the edge. 2. Push one balloon into the bottle neck, stretching its mouth over the outside of the neck. 3. Tie a knot in the second balloon and cut off its wide top half. Stretch the knotted part over the open bottom of the bottle. 4. Tape it so it is airtight.
flow.say: We're going to build a lung. The balloon inside is the lung. The bottle neck is the windpipe. The stretchy balloon at the bottom is the diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Put one balloon inside the neck. Stretch the other over the bottom. That one is your diaphragm.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Bottle Lung. You build a model lung from a bottle and two balloons.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the bottle with one hand. 2. With the other, they pull the knot of the bottom balloon gently down. 3. Watch the inside balloon. 4. Then let go.
flow.say: Pull the bottom balloon down, slowly. What happens to the lung? Now let go. What happens? This is what your diaphragm does every time you breathe.
flow.kid: Pull the bottom balloon down. What does the inside balloon do? Let go. What happens now?

ask.q: What happened when you pulled down?
good: The inside balloon filled up with air.
The lung got bigger.

ask.q: Why do you think it filled up?
good: Pulling down made more space inside the bottle, and air rushed in through the neck to fill the balloon.

check.q: In the bottle lung, you pulled the bottom balloon down and the inside balloon filled. What does the bottom balloon stand for?
options: The diaphragm, the muscle under the lungs
The nose
The heart
check.why: The bottom balloon is the diaphragm. In your body, it pulls down to make space, and air rushes into your lungs. Picking 'the nose' usually means thinking we suck air in with our nose. The nose is just the door. The pulling is done by the diaphragm.

flow.context: This is the step where you pull the bottom balloon and watch the model lung fill with air.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts a hand on their belly and breathes in deeply. 2. Compare it with the bottle lung. 3. Talk about what the model gets right and what it gets wrong.
flow.say: Every model is a little wrong. Real lungs aren't one balloon. They're like a sponge with 480 million tiny bubbles. What else is different in your body?
flow.kid: Breathe in deeply. Feel your belly push out. That's your diaphragm pulling down. How is the bottle different from your real lungs?

ask.q: How is the model different from real lungs?
good: We have two lungs, not one.
Real lungs are spongy, with millions of tiny bubbles.
Our ribs move too.
There is blood all around real lungs.

flow.parent: Children love finding what's wrong with a model. It's real science thinking: a model shows one idea, not everything.
flow.think: A fish has no diaphragm. How do they move water over their gills?
flow.context: This is the step where you compare the bottle lung with your own breathing, and find what the model gets wrong.

activities.title: Gill Watch: count a fish's breaths

materials.item: a fish to watch: a home aquarium, an aquarium shop, a pond, or live fish at the market
a phone or clock to time one minute
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Stay with a grown-up near ponds and tanks. Do not tap on aquarium glass. At a fish market, only look, and wash hands if you touch anything.

schedule.what: Gill Watch: count a fish's breaths

activities.record: Write how many times the fish's gill covers opened in one minute. Draw the fish and colour their gills.
activities.context: In this activity you watch a live fish and count how many times their gill covers open in one minute. If you can, you also look at the red gills of a fish at the market.

setup.art: A child kneeling in front of a home fish tank, watching a goldfish whose gill flaps are opening, a timer in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Watch the flaps behind a fish's eyes open and shut.

setup.art: A child making a tally mark in a notebook for each flap.
setup.caption: 2. Count each opening for one minute.

setup.art: A fish seller at an Indian market lifting the gill cover of a fresh fish to show bright red gills.
setup.caption: 3. At the market, look at the red gills under the flap.

flow.do: 1. Find one fish that is calm. 2. Look just behind their eyes at the gill covers, the flaps on each side. 3. Watch their mouth open and shut. 4. Count each time the gill covers open, for one minute, making a tally mark each time.
flow.say: See the flaps behind their eyes? That's where the water goes out. It comes in at the mouth and goes out there, over the gills. Let's count how many times they open in one minute.
flow.kid: Look behind the fish's eyes. See the flaps? They open and shut. Count each opening for one minute. Make a tally mark each time.
flow.parent: Small fish in warm water often open their gill covers 60 to 100 times a minute, much faster than we breathe. Counting is hard, so 30 seconds doubled is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gill Watch. You count how many times a fish's gill covers open in one minute.

flow.do: If you can, visit a fish market or ask at the fish counter. Ask the seller to lift the gill cover of a fresh fish. Look at the colour and shape of the gills.
flow.say: Fish sellers lift the gill flap to show how fresh a fish is. Bright red gills mean fresh. Why do you think they're so red?
flow.kid: Look under the flap of a fresh fish. See the red gills? They look like a comb with many thin teeth.

ask.q: Why are gills so red?
good: They are full of blood.
Blood comes close to the water there to pick up oxygen.

ask.q: Why do they have so many thin parts?
good: To have lots of surface, so they can catch more oxygen.

flow.context: This is the step where you look at the red gills of a fresh fish at the market.

flow.do: Compare the fish's count with your own breath count from the Breath Count experiment, if you did it.
flow.say: You took about 20 breaths a minute sitting still. The fish moved water over their gills many more times. Why might a fish have to work harder?
flow.kid: Was the fish's number bigger or smaller than yours? Why might a fish breathe so fast?

check.q: A small fish opened their gill covers 80 times a minute. You took 20 breaths. Why might the fish need so many?
options: Water has much less oxygen than air, so the fish moves lots of water
Fish are always frightened
Fish do not need oxygen, they just like moving water
check.why: Water holds far less oxygen than air, about thirty times less in the same space. So a fish must push a lot of water over their gills to get enough. Picking 'frightened' is a fair guess for a fish that's being watched, which is why we watch quietly. Picking 'fish don't need oxygen' is a common idea, but every animal needs oxygen.

flow.context: This is the last step of Gill Watch. You compare a fish's breathing with your own.

activities.title: Flat or Frilly? The gill shape test

materials.item: two sheets of kitchen paper towel, the same size
scissors
two clothes pegs and a string, or a clothes-drying stand
a bowl of water
a phone or clock

activities.safety: Use child-safe scissors. Wipe up any spilled water.

schedule.what: Flat or Frilly? The gill shape test

activities.record: Write which towel dried first and how long each took. Draw both and label which is like a gill.
activities.context: In this activity you test why gills and lungs are frilly and folded. You wet two paper towels and see whether a crumpled one or a frilly cut one dries faster.

setup.art: Two identical paper towels, one crumpled into a tight ball, one cut into many thin frilly strips still joined at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Crumple one towel into a ball. Cut the other into frilly strips.

setup.art: Both towels being dipped in a bowl of water, then hung side by side with clothes pegs on a string.
setup.caption: 2. Wet both. Hang them side by side.

setup.art: A child touching the frilly towel, which is dry, while the crumpled ball is still dark and wet, a timer showing 40 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Check every 10 minutes. Which one dries first?

flow.do: 1. Take two paper towels the same size. 2. Crumple one tightly into a ball. 3. Cut the other into thin strips, like a comb, leaving the top edge joined. 4. Dip both in water for 5 seconds. Lift them out and let them drip for 10 seconds. Don't squeeze them, or the strips will tear. 5. Hang them side by side, under a fan if you have one.
flow.say: Water leaves a wet towel through its surface, the outside that touches the air. Gills and lungs take oxygen in through their surface too. Which towel do you think has more surface touching the air?
flow.kid: Crumple one towel into a ball. Cut the other into thin strips. Wet both. Hang them up. Which one has more outside touching the air?

ask.q: Which towel will dry first? Why?
good: The frilly one, because more of it touches the air.
The frilly one, because the ball is all squashed inside.

flow.context: This is the first step of the gill shape test. You make one crumpled towel and one frilly towel and hang them up wet.

flow.do: Every 10 minutes, for about 40 minutes, gently touch both towels and note how they feel: wet, damp or dry. Each check takes a minute, so do something else in between.
flow.say: Let's check. Touch them gently. Which feels drier? The water is leaving through the surface, just as oxygen enters through the surface of a gill.
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, touch both towels. Wet, damp or dry? Write it down.
flow.parent: The frilly towel usually dries much faster, often in half the time or less. Same paper, same dip in water. Only the shape changed. That's why it's a fair test.
flow.context: This is the step where you check the two towels every 10 minutes to see which dries first.

flow.do: Talk about what the result means for gills and lungs.
flow.say: Same paper, same water, but the frilly one let the water out much faster. Gills are frilly. Lungs have millions of tiny bubbles. What's the trick?
flow.kid: The frilly one dried faster. Gills are frilly too. Lungs have millions of tiny bubbles. Why?

check.q: In the towel test, the frilly towel dried faster than the crumpled ball. What does this tell us about gills?
options: Gills are frilly so that lots of surface can take in oxygen fast
Gills are frilly to look pretty
Gills are frilly because fish are always wet
check.why: More surface means more can pass through at once. Water left the frilly towel faster, and oxygen gets into frilly gills faster. Picking 'look pretty' is a fun answer, but body parts usually have shapes that help them work. Picking 'always wet' is half right. Gills do need to stay wet, but the frills are about surface.

flow.think: Out of water, a fish's gill threads stick together, like the crumpled towel. What happens to their surface then?
flow.context: This is the last step of the gill shape test. You work out why gills and lungs are frilly.

activities.title: Follow Your Nose: find the snack by smell

materials.item: five small steel bowls or cups, with paper covers that have small holes poked in them
a smelly snack, like a piece of banana, a crushed elaichi pod or a little vanilla essence on cotton
a cloth for a blindfold

activities.safety: Walk slowly when blindfolded, on a clear floor. A grown-up guides.

schedule.what: Follow Your Nose: find the snack by smell

activities.record: Write how many tries it took to find the snack by smell. Write which animal you would like to have the nose of, and why.
activities.context: In this activity you try to find a hidden snack only by smell, the way a dog or an ant does. Then you compare your nose with animal noses.

setup.art: Five covered steel bowls in a row on a floor, one hiding a piece of banana, paper covers with small holes.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides a smelly snack in one of five covered bowls.

setup.art: A blindfolded child on hands and knees, sniffing each bowl in turn like a dog.
setup.caption: 2. Wear a blindfold. Sniff each bowl.

setup.art: The child lifting the blindfold and pointing at the right bowl, smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Point to the bowl you think has the snack.

flow.do: 1. While your child is out of the room, put the snack in one bowl and cover all five. 2. Blindfold your child. 3. They sniff each bowl and choose one. 4. Try 3 rounds with different snacks.
flow.say: You're going to be a dog for a minute. A dog finds food mostly by smell. Sniff each bowl. Which one hides the snack?
flow.kid: Put on the blindfold. Sniff each bowl, one by one. Which one has the snack? Point to it.

ask.q: Was it easy or hard?
good: Hard, my nose is not very strong.
Easy for the banana, hard for the elaichi.

flow.context: This is the first step of Follow Your Nose. You try to find a hidden snack only by smell.

flow.do: Talk about animal noses and other senses.
flow.say: A dog's nose is far, far better than ours. It can follow a smell trail days old. A mosquito finds you by the carbon dioxide you breathe out. A bat finds a moth by the echo. Which sense would help you most to find food in the dark?
flow.kid: A dog could find it at once. A mosquito smells your breath. A bat hears echoes. Which sense would you pick?

check.q: A mosquito finds people in a dark room. Which of these helps them most?
options: Smelling the carbon dioxide we breathe out, and sensing our warmth
Seeing us clearly in the dark
Hearing our hearts beat
check.why: Mosquitoes sense carbon dioxide in breath from a long way off, then use warmth and smell close up. Picking 'seeing clearly' is a natural guess, because we rely on our eyes. But many animals rely on other senses. Picking 'hearts beat' is creative, but heartbeats are far too quiet for a mosquito.

flow.context: This is the step where you compare your nose with animals' senses for finding food.

activities.title: How Long Can a Breath Last?

materials.item: a phone or clock with a seconds hand
a notebook to record times

activities.safety: Do this sitting down, on dry land, never in water. Hold only as long as is comfortable, never until it hurts. Stop at once if you feel dizzy. Children with asthma or heart problems should skip the holding and just do the timing for others.

schedule.what: How Long Can a Breath Last?

activities.record: Write your comfortable breath-hold time and the times of others in the family. Compare them with the animal times on the chart.
activities.context: In this activity you time how long you can comfortably hold your breath. Then you compare it with animals that hold their breath to hunt underwater.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat, cheeks gently closed, a grown-up holding a timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit down. Take a normal breath. Hold it, comfortably.

setup.art: The grown-up writing times in a notebook while a grandparent takes a turn.
setup.caption: 2. Time everyone in the family. Write down the times.

setup.art: A picture chart comparing a child, a Ganges river dolphin, a sea turtle and a sperm whale, each with a clock.
setup.caption: 3. Compare with animals that hunt underwater.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits cross-legged. 2. They take one normal breath, not a huge one, and hold it. 3. Time how long they hold it comfortably. 4. Stop the moment it feels uncomfortable. 5. Time each family member.
flow.say: Sit tall. Take a normal breath, and hold it gently. Don't push yourself. The moment you want to breathe, breathe. It's not a race to hurt. It's to notice.
flow.kid: Sit tall. Take a normal breath. Hold it gently. Breathe the moment you want to. Never push.
flow.parent: Most children can comfortably hold for 15 to 40 seconds. The urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up in the blood, not from running out of oxygen. Never let this become a contest to hold too long, and never do it in water.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Long Can a Breath Last? You time a comfortable breath-hold, sitting down.

flow.do: Show the chart of animal breath-holds and talk about it.
flow.say: The Ganges river dolphin comes up every minute or two. Some whales stay down for over an hour. How do they do it? They store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles, and slow their hearts down.
flow.kid: Look at the animals. A river dolphin holds their breath for one or two minutes. Some whales hold for over an hour!

chart.title: How long some air-breathing animals often stay underwater

check.q: Ganges river dolphins live in rivers all their lives. Why must they keep coming up?
options: They breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole
They come up to look around
They come up to drink rain
check.why: Dolphins have lungs, not gills. They can only get oxygen from air, through the blowhole on top of the head. Picking 'look around' is a fair guess, because many animals pop up to look. But Ganges river dolphins are nearly blind and find food by echoes. They come up to breathe.

flow.context: This is the step where you compare your breath-hold with animals that hold their breath to hunt underwater.

activities.title: Mouth Tools Buffet

materials.item: tools: a straw, a tea strainer, a clothes peg, a pair of tweezers or two ice-cream sticks, a spoon
foods: a bowl of water or juice, a bowl of water with puffed rice floating in it, a few cooked noodles hidden in a tray of dry atta, some peanuts
a phone or clock to time 30 seconds

activities.safety: Use clean tools if you plan to eat any food. Don't run with the tweezers or sticks.
activities.record: Make a table: tool, which food it was best at, and which animal has a mouth like that tool.
activities.context: In this activity you pretend different kitchen tools are animal mouths. You find which tool is best at which food, to see how animal mouths fit the way they get food.

setup.art: A table with a straw, a tea strainer, a clothes peg, tweezers and a spoon, and bowls of juice, floating puffed rice, noodles in atta and peanuts.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the tool mouths and the foods.

setup.art: A child using a tea strainer to scoop floating puffed rice out of water, like a flamingo.
setup.caption: 2. Try each tool on each food for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A chart with pictures matching the straw to a butterfly, the strainer to a flamingo, the tweezers to a heron and the peg to a parrot.
setup.caption: 3. Match each tool to an animal with that kind of mouth.

flow.do: 1. Set out the foods. 2. Your child tries each tool on each food for 30 seconds. 3. Count how many pieces they collect, or how much juice they drink. 4. Write the best tool for each food.
flow.say: Each tool is a pretend animal mouth. You have 30 seconds with each one. Which mouth is best for which food?
flow.kid: Each tool is an animal mouth. Try each one on each food. You get 30 seconds. Which is best?

ask.q: Which tool was best at the noodles in the atta?
good: The tweezers or sticks, like a long beak poking in mud.

ask.q: Which was best at the floating puffed rice?
good: The tea strainer, because the water runs out and the food stays.

flow.context: This is the first step of Mouth Tools Buffet. You try kitchen tools as pretend animal mouths on different foods.

flow.do: Match each tool to an animal and talk about it.
flow.say: Your straw is like a butterfly's long tongue, sipping nectar. The strainer is like a flamingo's beak, sieving tiny food. The tweezers are like a heron's long beak, picking up food. The peg is like a parrot's strong beak, gripping a nut.
flow.kid: Straw: butterfly. Strainer: flamingo. Tweezers: heron. Peg: parrot. Which was your favourite?

check.q: A flamingo eats tiny shrimps floating in lake water. In the buffet, which tool worked like their beak?
options: The tea strainer
The straw
The clothes peg
check.why: A flamingo's beak works like a sieve. Water goes out, and tiny food stays in. That's filter feeding. Picking 'the straw' would suck up water and food together, and the flamingo would get mostly water. Picking 'the peg' is good for one big thing at a time, not many tiny ones.

flow.context: This is the step where you match each tool to an animal whose mouth works the same way.

projects.title: My Breath Diary

materials.item: a notebook for the diary
a phone or clock to time one minute
coloured pencils

projects.safety: Count breaths only. Never hold the breath for this project.

schedule.what: Make the diary table. Count breaths for one minute on waking and before bed.
Count breaths on waking, after playing outside, and before bed.
Count breaths while reading, after climbing stairs, and while a grown-up counts yours while you sleep.
Count the breaths of a pet, a sleeping sibling or a grandparent, with permission.
Draw a line chart of your breaths at each time. Write what you found.

projects.record: A table of breath counts at different times of day, and a line chart. Write when you breathed fastest and slowest, and why.
projects.context: In this 5-day project you keep a diary of how many breaths you take in one minute at different times, like waking up, playing and sleeping, and draw a chart.

setup.art: A child sitting up in bed at dawn with a hand on the chest, a small notebook open on the blanket.
setup.caption: 1. Count your breaths for one minute when you wake up.

setup.art: The child sitting on stairs after climbing, panting, a grown-up timing.
setup.caption: 2. Count again after playing or climbing stairs.

setup.art: A notebook with a line chart going up and down across the times of day.
setup.caption: 3. After 5 days, draw a line chart of all your counts.

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Draw a table with columns: day, time, what I was doing, breaths in one minute. 2. Count on waking and before bed.
flow.say: For five days, you'll be a breath scientist. Each day we'll count your breaths at different times. At the end we'll see when you breathe fastest and slowest.
flow.kid: Draw your diary table. Count your breaths when you wake up. Count again before bed.
flow.context: This is the first day of My Breath Diary. You make the table and do the first two counts.

flow.do: Days 2 to 4. Do the day's counts and write them in. On day 3, a grown-up counts the child's breaths while asleep. On day 4, count a pet or another family member.
flow.say: Today's counts are in the diary plan. Remember, sit the same way each time, and count for one whole minute.
flow.kid: Do today's counts. Write each one in your table. Count for one whole minute.
flow.parent: Sleeping breaths are usually slowest. A cat or dog at rest often breathes 20 to 30 times a minute. Small animals breathe faster than big ones.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of My Breath Diary. You count your breaths at different times each day.

flow.do: Day 5. 1. Draw a line chart with the times along the bottom and breaths up the side. 2. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's draw a line chart. Each dot is one count. When was the line highest? When was it lowest? Why?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each count. Join the dots. When was the line highest? Why?

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute during a day
chart.note: Made-up numbers, to show what a chart can look like.

check.q: In the breath diary chart, the line is highest just after climbing stairs. Why?
options: Leg muscles were working hard and needed more oxygen
Stairs have less air
We breathe faster when we are bored
check.why: Hard-working muscles use more oxygen, so you breathe faster to bring more in. Picking 'stairs have less air' mixes this up with high mountains, where air really is thinner. A few stairs make no difference to the air.

flow.context: This is the last day of My Breath Diary. You draw a line chart and explain it.

challenges.title: Design a River-Bottom Hunter
challenges.problem: Imagine a new animal that lives at the bottom of a deep, muddy river, like the Ganga. The water is so brown that it is dark even at noon, and in summer it has very little oxygen. Design an animal that can breathe and find food there.
constraints: Your animal must get enough oxygen, even in summer.
It must find food in water too muddy to see through.
Draw it, label every special part, and say what it eats and how.
materials: clay or play dough, if you want to make a model
pictures of real river animals, if you have them
general: Give them lungs and let them come up to breathe, like the Ganges river dolphin.
Give them gills plus a way to gulp air, like the climbing perch and magur catfish.
Give them whiskers that feel and taste, like a catfish, or echolocation clicks like a dolphin.
creative: The Ganges river dolphin is nearly blind. They swim on their side, sweeping their long beak through the mud, and finds fish with clicks.
Some fish make weak electricity around their bodies and feel when something disturbs it. Could your animal do that?
Could your animal carry an air bubble with them, like the water spiders that live in silk bubbles underwater?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own river-bottom hunter. Give them a name. Draw them, label them, and explain to your family how they breathe and how they find food.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent an animal that can breathe and find food at the bottom of a dark, muddy river.

setup.art: A cross-section of a brown, murky river with little light reaching the bottom and a few fish in the mud.
setup.caption: 1. Picture the dark, muddy river bottom.

setup.art: A child drawing an invented animal with labels for whiskers, gills and a breathing tube.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your animal. Label their breathing and food-finding parts.

setup.art: The child holding up the drawing and explaining it to a grandparent.
setup.caption: 3. Explain your design to someone.

flow.do: Read the problem with your child and talk about the two problems: little oxygen, and no light.
flow.say: Two problems. One: there isn't much oxygen in the water. Two: it's too dark and muddy to see. What could a body do about each one?
flow.kid: Your animal lives in a dark, muddy river. Two problems: little oxygen, and no light. How could a body solve them?

ask.q: How could they get more oxygen?
good: Come up and breathe air.
Have extra big gills.
Gulp air like the climbing perch.

ask.q: How could they find food in the dark?
good: Smell or taste the water.
Use whiskers.
Use clicks and echoes.

flow.context: This is the first step of Design a River-Bottom Hunter. You think about the two problems your animal must solve.

flow.do: Your child draws the animal and labels each special part.
flow.say: Draw your animal. Label every part that helps them breathe or find food. Then give them a name.
flow.kid: Draw your animal. Label their breathing parts. Label their food-finding parts. Give them a name.

check.q: In a dark, muddy river, which sense would help an animal least to find food?
options: Sharp eyesight
Echolocation clicks
Feeling whiskers
check.why: In water too muddy to see through, eyes don't help much. That's why the Ganges river dolphin's eyes are tiny, and they use clicks instead. Picking 'echolocation' or 'whiskers' means choosing a sense that works well in the dark, which is a smart choice, but the question asks which helps least.

flow.context: This is the step where you draw and label your river-bottom hunter.

flow.do: Your child explains the design to someone in the family.
flow.say: Tell Paati or a friend about your animal. How do they breathe? How do they find food? What would happen to them if the river got dirtier?
flow.kid: Show your drawing to someone. Explain how they breathe and find food.
flow.think: Real Ganges river dolphins are in danger. The water is dirtier, and dams block their way. How could people help them?
flow.context: This is the last step of Design a River-Bottom Hunter. You explain your design to someone.

challenges.title: Build a Filter-Feeder's Sieve
challenges.problem: Flamingos and whale sharks sieve tiny bits of food out of the water flowing past them. A good sieve must catch the food and still let the water through quickly. Build a filter that catches the used tea leaves from one jug of water, and lets the water through as fast as possible.
constraints: Use one jug of water with one spoon of used tea leaves stirred in.
Pour it through your filter into a bowl in one steady pour.
Time how long the water takes to pass through, and look in the bowl for leaves that got through.
materials: a jug of water and a spoon of used tea leaves
filter materials: a cotton handkerchief, a tea strainer, a comb, a sponge, cotton wool, a folded paper towel
a funnel made from a cut plastic bottle
general: A tea strainer lets water through fast, but tiny bits of leaf get through too.
A cloth catches every bit, but water flows through it slowly.
Two filters, a coarse one first and a fine one second, can catch more without clogging.
creative: Fold the cloth into pleats, so there is more cloth for the water to pass through in the same funnel.
A fish's gills are also folded into many thin threads, so that a lot of water touches a lot of surface. Can your filter give the water more surface?
Flamingos pump water through their beaks with their tongues. Can you help the water through without pushing the leaves through too?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own filter. Draw it, test it, and time it. Can you beat your best design?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a filter that catches used tea leaves from water, to see why sieving mouths and gills have so much surface.

setup.art: A jug of water with used tea leaves swirling in it, next to a funnel made from a cut plastic bottle over a bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Stir used tea leaves into a jug of water.

setup.art: A pleated cotton handkerchief inside the bottle funnel, water being poured through it into a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the water through your filter.

setup.art: A child timing the pour with a phone while tea-leaf water drips through a pleated cloth in a bottle funnel.
setup.caption: 3. Time the pour. Look for leaves in the bowl.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the top off a plastic bottle to make a funnel. 2. Stir one spoon of used tea leaves into a jug of water. 3. Try the tea strainer first, as the test to beat.
flow.say: Let's start with the tea strainer. Pour slowly. How long did the water take? Did any bits of leaf get into the bowl?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a funnel. Pour the tea water through a tea strainer. Time it. Did leaves get through?
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Filter-Feeder's Sieve. You test a tea strainer as the filter to beat.

flow.do: Your child designs, builds and tests two or three filters, timing each pour and checking the bowl for leaves.
flow.say: Now design your own. A cloth catches everything, but it is slow. How could you make water go through a cloth faster?
