check.q: A pleated cloth caught all the tea leaves, just like a flat cloth, but the water went through faster. Why?
options: Pleats give more cloth for the water to pass through
Pleats make the water colder
Pleated cloth is heavier
check.why: Folding the cloth into pleats packs more cloth into the same funnel, so more water can pass through at once. Gills are folded into many thin threads for the same reason: more surface lets more water touch them. Picking 'colder' or 'heavier' is guessing at other changes. We only changed the folding.

flow.context: This is the step where you design and test your own filters.

flow.do: Compare the designs. Talk about how real gills differ from filters.
flow.say: Real gills don't trap oxygen like leaves. Oxygen passes through thin walls into blood. But both need lots of surface, with lots of water flowing past.
flow.kid: Which filter was fastest? Real gills also have lots of surface.
flow.think: A filter catches things. A gill lets oxygen pass through into blood. How are they alike, and how are they different?

quiz.p: A dog is fast asleep and not moving at all. Why does she still breathe?
opts: Her cells still need oxygen to get energy from food, even in sleep
To keep her nose wet
She doesn't. Animals stop breathing in sleep
quiz.why: Even asleep, a dog's heart beats, her brain works and her body stays warm. All of that uses energy, so her cells keep using oxygen. She just breathes more slowly than when she runs.

quiz.p: How does a fish get oxygen?
opts: Water flows in at their mouth, over their gills, and out under the gill covers
They come to the surface to breathe air, like a dolphin
They don't need oxygen
quiz.why: Fish pump water over their gills, which take oxygen out of the water. Picking 'like a dolphin' mixes up fish and dolphins. Dolphins have lungs and must come up for air.

quiz.p: Lungs, gills and breathing skin are all…
opts: Thin, damp and close to blood
Hard and dry
Only found in fish
quiz.why: Oxygen can only pass through a thin, wet wall into blood. Picking 'hard and dry' is the opposite. A dry surface can't let oxygen in, which is why fish die out of water and worms die in the sun.

quiz.p: An earthworm is left on a hot, dry path in the sun. Why is that dangerous for them?
opts: Their skin dries out, and they breathe through their skin
They get sunburned on their gills
They can't see the way home
quiz.why: Earthworms breathe through damp skin. If the skin dries, oxygen can't get through. Picking 'gills' is a mix-up. Earthworms have no gills.

quiz.p: You counted 20 breaths a minute sitting still, and 40 after jumping. What is the best explanation?
opts: Working muscles need more oxygen, so we breathe faster
Jumping makes the lungs bigger
The timer ran faster
quiz.why: Muscles working hard use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, so we breathe faster. Picking 'timer ran faster' is a good scientist's worry. That's why we used the same timer each time and counted three times.
quiz.context: In the Breath Count experiment, you counted breaths for one minute sitting still, then after jumping.

quiz.p: In the limewater test, breathed-out air made the water milky fast. Room air did not. What does this show?
opts: Breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide than room air
Breathed-out air has no oxygen
Limewater is broken
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Breathed-out air carries carbon dioxide from your cells. Picking 'no oxygen' is a common mistake. Breathed-out air still has about 16 parts in 100 oxygen.
quiz.context: In the Limewater Test, you bubbled breath into one glass of limewater and pushed room air from a squeezed bottle into the other.

quiz.p: Which animal finds their food mostly by echoes?
opts: A bat
An eagle
A cow
quiz.why: Bats send out high sounds and listen for echoes. Eagles use sharp eyes. Cows graze on grass they can see and smell.

quiz.p: A pit viper hunts mice in the dark. Which special sense helps them?
opts: Pits on their face that sense warmth
Echolocation
Very sharp hearing in big ears
quiz.why: Pit vipers, like the Malabar pit viper of the Western Ghats, have pits that feel the warmth of a mouse. Picking 'echolocation' mixes it up with bats. Snakes don't have outer ears at all.

quiz.p: A vulture eats animals that have already died. What kind of eater is the vulture?
opts: A scavenger
A filter feeder
A grazer
quiz.why: A scavenger eats the dead. Vultures keep the land clean and stop disease from spreading. A filter feeder sieves water. A grazer eats plants.

quiz.p: A spider builds a sticky web and waits. How do they get food?
opts: By trapping
By grazing
By filtering water
quiz.why: A web is a trap. Flying insects get stuck, and the spider eats them. Grazing means eating plants for hours. Filtering means sieving water.

quiz.p: Why do earthworms come out onto roads after rain?
opts: Scientists are not sure. There are several ideas
To drink rainwater
Because they are lost
quiz.why: Scientists still argue. Some think the worms need air, some think it's a good time to travel, and some think rain sounds like a hungry mole. Picking a simple answer is natural. But this is a real open question.

quiz.p: Where did the oxygen in the air come from?
opts: Plants on land and tiny algae in the sea made it
It has always been there since the Earth began
Volcanoes puff it out
quiz.why: Living things that make food from sunlight give out oxygen. More than two billion years ago, tiny living things in the sea began filling the air with it. Picking 'always there' is a common idea, but ancient rocks show the early air had almost no oxygen.

quiz.p: Your lungs bring oxygen in. Which parts of you actually use it?
opts: Almost every cell in your body
Only your lungs
Only your heart
quiz.why: The lungs are like a door. The blood carries oxygen to the cells, from your toes to your brain. Each cell uses it to get energy from food. Picking 'only lungs' is the most common mix-up. Taking in oxygen and using it happen in different places.

quiz.p: Plants take in carbon dioxide to make their food. You breathe carbon dioxide out. What does this mean?
opts: Some carbon from the food you ate can end up in a plant's leaf
Plants and people never share anything
Plants make carbon dioxide for us to breathe
quiz.why: The carbon in your breath came from your food. A plant can take in that carbon dioxide and build it into a new leaf. Picking 'plants make carbon dioxide for us' gets it backwards. Plants give out oxygen in sunlight.

applications: Doctors count breaths per minute to check if a person is unwell. Fast breathing at rest can be a sign of illness.
Hospitals give oxygen through masks to people whose lungs are not working well.
Divers carry tanks of air because people cannot take oxygen from water.
Fish farmers in India bubble air into ponds in hot weather, so the fish don't run short of oxygen.
Aquarium pumps push air bubbles into fish tanks for the same reason.
Sniffer dogs at airports and with the police find hidden things by smell.
Ships and submarines use sonar, which sends out sounds and listens for echoes, just like bats and dolphins.
Mosquito traps use carbon dioxide or warmth to lure mosquitoes, because that is how mosquitoes find people.
Fish sellers and buyers check bright red gills to see if fish is fresh.
Pranayama and slow breathing are used to calm the body and mind.
Scientists measure the oxygen in rivers to check how healthy the water is for fish.
During operations, doctors measure the carbon dioxide in a patient's breath, to check that the body is using oxygen and the lungs are working.

open_questions.q: Why do earthworms crawl onto roads after rain?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas: to breathe, to travel, or to escape moles. Experiments support different ideas, and it may be a mix.

open_questions.q: Did lungs come before swim bladders, or swim bladders before lungs?
open_questions.why_open: Most evidence now points to lungs first. But the earliest steps happened over 400 million years ago, and fossils of soft lungs are rare.

open_questions.q: How do deep-diving whales stay underwater for hours without harm?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the tricks, like storing oxygen in muscles and slowing the heart. But whales are hard to study deep in the ocean, so much is still unknown.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a dog's nose tell apart so many smells?
open_questions.why_open: We know dogs have many more smell cells than us. But how the brain sorts millions of smell mixtures is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why were some insects giant long ago?
open_questions.why_open: About 300 million years ago there were dragonfly-like insects with wings a little wider than two school rulers end to end. Some scientists think the air had more oxygen then, which helped insects' air pipes. Others think there were other reasons.

open_questions.q: How do bar-headed geese fly in such thin air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that their blood, lungs and hearts are special. But how they manage the hardest climbs is still studied.

open_questions.q: Can people learn to echolocate like bats?
open_questions.why_open: Some blind people use tongue clicks to find their way, and studies show it works. How well people can learn it, and how the brain does it, is still being studied.

maths.problem: You counted your breaths for 15 seconds and got 5. A minute has four lots of 15 seconds. How many breaths would that be in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 seconds, so four lots of 15 seconds. You took 5 breaths in each lot. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Or 4 times 5 is 20.
maths.context: This is about the Breath Count experiment. You count your breaths while sitting still. Counting for a full minute is hard, so you can count for 15 seconds and work out the rest.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a short time and multiplying saves time, and scientists and doctors use this trick to count breaths and heartbeats.

maths.problem: Look at the chart. Sitting still you took 20 breaths a minute. After jumping you took 40. How many times as many breaths did you take after jumping?
maths.explain: After jumping the bar shows 40. Sitting still it shows 20. 40 divided by 20 is 2. So you breathed twice as many times. Check: 20 + 20 = 40.
maths.context: This is about the Breath Count experiment, where you counted breaths sitting still and just after jumping one minute.

chart.title: Made-up results: breaths in one minute

maths.why_maths: Saying 'twice as many' tells us how big the change is, which is more useful than just saying 'more'.

maths.problem: A small fish opened their gill covers 40 times in 30 seconds. How many times would that be in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is two lots of 30 seconds. 40 + 40 = 80. So the fish opened their gill covers 80 times a minute. That is 4 times as many as a child's 20 breaths.
maths.context: This is about Gill Watch, where you counted how many times a fish's gill covers opened.
maths.why_maths: Turning counts into 'per minute' lets us compare a fish's breathing fairly with our own.

maths.problem: Look at the ant chart. How many ants came to the three baits altogether after 30 minutes? How many more ants were on the sugar than on the salt?
maths.answer: 40 ants altogether. 23 more on the sugar than on the salt.
maths.explain: Sugar 24, biscuit 15 and salt 1. 24 + 15 = 39, and 39 + 1 = 40 altogether. Sugar minus salt is 24 take away 1, which is 23.
maths.context: This is about Ant Detectives. You put sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path and counted the ants on each after 30 minutes.

chart.title: Made-up results: ants on each bait after 30 minutes

maths.why_maths: Adding up and comparing bars tells us clearly which food the ants liked most, and by how much.

maths.problem: In the breath diary, you breathed 16 times a minute asleep and 34 times a minute after climbing stairs. What is the difference?
maths.explain: 34 take away 16. 34 take away 10 is 24. 24 take away 6 is 18. So you breathed 18 more times a minute after the stairs.
maths.context: This is about My Breath Diary, where you counted your breaths at different times of day for five days.

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute during a day

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much your body changes its breathing to match what you are doing.

maths.problem: In 10,000 drops of room air, about 4 are carbon dioxide. In 10,000 drops of breathed-out air, about 400 are carbon dioxide. How many times as much carbon dioxide is in your breath? Does that fit what you saw in the limewater test?
maths.answer: 100 times as much. Yes: the breath glass turned milky fast, and the room-air glass stayed almost clear.
maths.explain: 400 divided by 4 is 100, because 4 times 100 is 400. With 100 times as much carbon dioxide, breath turns limewater milky much faster than room air does.
maths.context: This is about the Limewater Test, where your breath turned limewater milky but room air hardly changed it.
maths.why_maths: A number like '100 times as much' explains why one glass went milky in a minute while the other stayed clear.

roots.context: We have seen what is in our breath, and how animals breathe and find food. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your breath turned clear limewater milky, but room air hardly changed it. The milkiness comes from carbon dioxide, which your cells make as they use food for energy. The carbon in that gas came from the food you ate. So part of every meal leaves your body in your breath.
deep_truth.habit: We think of eating and breathing as two separate jobs, and we think food leaves the body only as poo and wee. In fact, much of the food we digest leaves through the lungs. Eating and breathing meet in every cell.
deep_truth.evidence: In the limewater test, the glass with your breath turned milky within a minute, and the glass with room air stayed almost clear. Breathed-out air has about 100 times as much carbon dioxide as room air. In 2014, two scientists worked out that most of the fat a person loses leaves through the lungs, as carbon dioxide.

three.who_am_i: You are millions of millions of cells, and almost every one uses oxygen to get energy from food. The tiny parts that do this were once free-living bacteria.
three.what_is_life: To stay alive, an animal must keep finding food and keep breathing, because their cells use both all the time.
three.what_is_this_world: Plants use sunlight to make food and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water. Animals use that food and oxygen, and give the carbon dioxide back.

roots.thread: Plants use the Sun's light to join carbon dioxide and water into food, and they give out oxygen. Animals find that food with their senses, and take in that oxygen with lungs, gills or skin. Their cells join the two again, take out the energy, and breathe out carbon dioxide and water. Plants take those back in and use them again. So one circle of the same carbon, water and oxygen runs through every plant and animal, driven by the Sun.

teachings.teaching: The boy Bhrigu asks his father Varuna what the source of everything is. Bhrigu first understands that food is that source: from food all beings are born, by food they live, and into food they return. Then he understands that breath, prana, is the source too.
teachings.link: In this unit, food and breath meet in every cell. Your body is built from food, it uses oxygen to get energy from that food, and part of the food goes back out in your breath.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says that beings come from food, and food comes from rain. He calls this a wheel that keeps turning, in which each part gives to the next.
teachings.link: Science finds a circle too. Plants make food from rain water, air and light. Animals eat it, and breathe out the carbon dioxide that plants use to make more food.

science.text: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things that use sunlight: tiny living things in the sea first, more than two billion years ago, then plants. Today, roughly half still comes from tiny algae in the sea.
The tiny parts inside our cells that use oxygen, called mitochondria, came from bacteria that started living inside bigger cells long ago.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that a body is only earth, water, fire and air, put together. Many scientists today say something similar: breathing is chemistry, gases passing through thin walls and food broken down in cells. On this view, nothing more is needed to explain it. That is an honest view, and it explains breathing well.

practice.title: Breath and the meal
practice.say: Let's sit tall and close our eyes. Hold your hand in front of your mouth. Breathe out slowly, and feel the warm air on your palm. Now think of what you ate today. Now open your eyes. Where will that breath go next?

how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, many people followed the Greek thinker Aristotle, and later the doctor Galen. They taught that we breathe mainly to cool the heat of the heart. In the 1750s, the Scottish chemist Joseph Black found a gas he called 'fixed air'. It turned limewater milky. He found that breath turns limewater milky too, so breath carries fixed air. Today we call it carbon dioxide. In the 1770s and 1780s, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier worked out what breathing does. With Pierre-Simon Laplace, he put a guinea pig in a box packed with ice. The animal's warmth melted the ice, and they breathed out carbon dioxide, like a slowly burning candle. So, Lavoisier said, breathing feeds a slow burning inside the body, which uses oxygen from the air. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked beside him. She kept the lab notes, translated science from English, and drew the experiments on people breathing into masks. Breathing does not cool the heart. It brings in oxygen to use food, and carries the carbon dioxide away.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Black, Antoine Lavoisier, Pierre-Simon Laplace and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier
how_we_found_out.when: 1750s (Black's fixed air), 1783 (the guinea pig in ice), about 1790 (Marie-Anne Lavoisier's drawings of breathing experiments)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle and Galen taught that breathing is mainly for cooling the heart. Black showed that breath carries carbon dioxide, and Lavoisier showed that an animal uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and heat, like a slow fire.
